subtopic: MARITIME PROVINCE LUMBER WORKERS EMPLOYED IN THE UNITED STATES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MARITIME PROVINCE LUMBER WORKERS EMPLOYED IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
A question was asked on Thursday last by the hon. member for Northumberland, N.B. (Mr. O'Brien) in reference to the movement of Canadian lumbermen to work in the Maine woods. My hon. friend asked why permits had been issued to these young men to cross the border, and what action would be taken to stop this drain on Canadian man-poiver. I informed my hon. friend the leader of the opposition on Friday that I would give later on a more detailed statement than it was possible to give at that time. The facts, I am informed, are as follows:
Some 4,400 lumbermen, living for the most part in villages along the Maine-Quebec border, have been permitted by the United States immigration authorities to enter the United States temporarily and under bond to work in the Maine woods during the next few months. In view of the bonded guarantees that the individuals concerned will return to Canada before March 1, 1942, the United States authorities have waived the usual passport and visa requirement for this seasonal border movement. No question therefore arose of issuing Canadian passports to the individuals concerned.
The lumbering operations in which these men are employed are essential for the manufacture of high quality alpha pulp required by the defence industries of the United Kingdom and the United States. A good proportion of the Canadian lumbermen whose temporary entry into the United States was permitted, subject to the above conditions, are cutting pulpwood which is floated back to Canada down the St. John river, for manufacture into alpha pulp for export to the United Kingdom. A substantial part of the United States output of this product is also under contract to the United Kingdom.
The men taking this winter employment in Maine are of course all subject, within their respective age groups, to the proclamations issued under the national war service regulations.
In reply to the second question, I might add that consideration is being given at the moment to the whole problem of border control, of which this particular movement is but one aspect.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext:
Certain questions were
raised by the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Castleden) and the hon. member for Dan-forth (Mr. Harris) with respect to the special committee on war expenditures. I might give the house a brief statement as to how that matter stands and as to the powers of hon. members of the house to have a very full discussion with regard to these expenditures.
On June 10 last, the special committee on war expenditures was authorized by order of the house to sit, notwithstanding the adjournment of the house.
The committee met on July 7 and resolved itself into three subcommittees to inquire into various subjects, set out on page 549 of the Votes and Proceedings of Monday, November 3. These subcommittees sat for approximately seven weeks during July and August and held altogether eighty-three sittings and examined eighty-nine witnesses.
The reports of the subcommittees were carefully considered by the main committee, which agreed upon seven reports. These were all presented to the house on November 3.
In the fourth report the committee stated that in view of the importance and scope of the inquiry referred to the committee, it was recommended that the inquiry be continued and that for the said purpose, a committee be appointed at the next session.
With regard to the inquiry made by the hon. member for Yorkton, it should be pointed out that the government has no control over the committee which was appointed by the house and responsible to the house.
Furthermore, there is no need of extending the powers of the committee to enable it to investigate contracts let by the Department of Munitions and Supply. The committee has already the fullest possible powers in that regard. Indeed, there are no restrictions of any kind upon the powers of the committee to examine into any war expenditures. The whole field of inquiry into all war expenditures is open to the committee. It is, however, obvious that the committee cannot complete its examination into all subjects of inquiry at the same time.
An examination of the subjects of inquiry assigned to the various subcommittees will indicate that the committee has been concerning itself in the main with subjects relating to activities which have their origin in the several

Foreign Exchange
branches of the Department of National Defence. It might be noted that in respect of contracts let by the Department of Munitions and Supply, the latter department lets such contracts after it has received a contract demand from one of the Departments of National Defence. The committee has already made a considerable study of the operations of the Department of Munitions and Supply, but there is no doubt that a full inquiry into the subject of war contracts will be made by the committee when a new committee is established next session. The committee will be free to make the fullest possible examination into the subject of war contracts.
With regard to the questions of the hon. member for Danforth, it might be pointed out that subject to the arrangement that has been made between the leaders on both sides of the house, there is nothing in the way of procedure to restrict the right of any member to discuss the reports that were presented last Monday. It is suggested, however, that these reports are voluminous and contain a great many recommendations. It would seem desirable that there should be an opportunity of careful study of the recommendations by the departments concerned.
When the next session takes place it is the intention of the government, if the house agrees, to establish a committee to deal with the subject of war expenditures and on the motion made for the establishment of such a committee, there will be the fullest possible opportunity afforded to every member of the house who is interested in the subject of discussing the reports, the recommendations contained therein and indeed, the subject of economy in war expenditures in every possible phase. It would seem preferable that the debate on these reports should take place on such a motion.

I wish to bring before the committee a couple of matters, but before doing so I should like to go on record as registering my protest, which is all I can do at the present moment, against further restrictions on the rights of individual members by the announcement made last week that private members would not be allowed to follow the ordinary course in committee of the whole by moving motions or amendments, and so on. All of us, except the most recent members, are aware that in the course of the session we go into committee hundreds of times, and the procedure always is to discuss one specific item. We discuss a resolution on which some bill is to be founded, or we discuss the bill itself, and when we are in committee it is the option of anyone to move an amendment, to move to insert a new section, or anything of that kind.
I feel strongly tempted to ask you, Mr. Chairman, whether there is anything before the committee now, and I rather think that if I did your answer would be no. It is well known that when the Speaker is in the chair, or when the chairman of committees is presiding, there must be something before the house or the committee, as the case may be. If there is nothing before the chair the presiding officer immediately turns to the leader of the government to ascertain the next order of business to which the house or the committee shall proceed, and when the order paper is exhausted the house must adjourn. That, however, has not been done on this occasion.

I remember the leader of the opposition saying that it would have to be done by unanimous consent, but my submission is that it was not so done.

I did not object at that time because unanimous consent was not asked, and I must admit I was perhaps innocent in the matter; but I never dreamed for a moment that the ordinary procedure in committee would not be followed. I submit that we were to some extent led into a situation that has never happened before. However, I do not want to delay the committee or to argue about it. We are in a rather ridiculous position apart from being more or less unconstitutional. When we were young and went into the pantry we w'ere told by our mothers, "you may look but you must not touch." The position here is, "You may talk but you must not act." We shall be known as the parliament that did nothing and could do nothing.
The leader of the opposition the other day seemed to have the same idea, that everything was not according to Hoyle, when he said that members would be reduced to the position of a debating society. I differ with him in that regard; I think we are below the status of a debating society. In the debating

The War-Mr. Neill
society of our young days we used to meet to debate some very abstruse question, such as whether the pen was mightier than the sword. It might not have had any great effect on our day and generation but we did decide in favour either of the pen or of the sword. When the Ladies' Aid meet to discuss whether they shall lay down linoleum in the vicarage or in the manse, they come to some conclusion; they decide either to lay it down or not to lay it down. At any rate, they do something; they come to a definite decision. Never before have we been in such a situation as this and I cannot help asking myself why. Is the government afraid? What is it afraid of? Hon. gentlemen opposite have a huge and loyal majority behind them and if anyone moved a vote of want of confidence I am sure he would have the greatest difficulty in getting a member to second it. There is no question of defeating the government or of going to the country. What is the trouble? Is the Prime Minister afraid of private members? We are the representatives of the people of Canada. Already we have had cut off-and we all agreed to it in all loyalty-the opportunity of moving resolutions in this house during this session. We were told that it was necessary to save time. We agreed to that. Now we are to be allowed time but we must not have any action; we are not to take any action at all.
Now, dealing with the two matters I wanted to bring up, the first is the gasoline situation.' It is an illustration of the curious policies the government seem to adopt not only in this matter but in others; they begin by trusting the people too much and end by trusting them too little. The result is a middle-of-the-road wishy-washy policy that results in small achievement and a great deal of irritation. But in saying this I exempt the Minister of Finance. Anyone who listened to his very able speech the other night setting forth his policies must have realized that we were listening to a man of great ability. I congratulate him on having the brains to conceive such a policy and the courage to present it, a far-sighted, bold policy with great potentialities, I only hope that when it gets into the hands of the officials it will not be smothered in the red tape in which bureaucratic people always seem to love to envelop anything
As I say, the government started by trusting the people too much; they thought that if they told the people that gasoline restriction was necessary they would all voluntarily submit. But that turned out a complete failure. Then they went to the opposite extreme; they saw that compulsion was needed but they
got scared, thought the people would not accept the government's statement that it was necessary, and might be dissatisfied and express their dissatisfaction by their votes. So the matter was held off for months and much precious time was lost. The result of it all was a very small saving made by a very few instead of a large saving made by a great many people, and in addition there was a great deal of dissatisfaction and ill-will. The minister said the other day he thought they had done very well because in a certain month the restriction had produced, not a reduction in consumption, but a non-increase. That is, whereas the previous month's consumption had exceeded that of the corresponding month a year ago, this month it remained the same as the corresponding month last year. He thought that was substantial progress. Well, if the war situation needs gasoline-saving I think it is hardly satisfactory to record that we did not do any worse than a year ago. It reminds me of the man and woman who by dire necessity were compelled greatly to reduce their expenditure, and after much discussion and argument and a few tears they decided that the woman had to go without a sewing machine, whereupon the man went out and bought an expensive set of golf clubs, and the net result rvas that the common purse was no better off.
We have lost much precious time by following a circuitous route and have not got anywhere yet. They made a general appeal to the public and it proved to be as futile as any suggestion would be that we should pay our taxes without compulsion. Anyone with a knowledge of human nature would have expected just this. About ten per cent of the people-I do not give that as an exact figure, because I do not know, but a certain proportion, say ten per cent-can always be trusted to do the loyal, the right and the decent thing. Another ten per cent are so utterly and intensely selfish that they will do nothing that they are not compelled to do. It does not matter to them that they see their neighbours making the necessary sacrifice. In between there is the great mass, call them eighty per cent, who are anxious to do the right thing; they only need to be told, but they have a sense of fairness and proportion which causes them to say: "I am willing to do it, but it has to be done all round. I am not going to do it and see Tom Jones, who is better able to make the sacrifice, evading it." So the government saw that compulsion was necessary, but they were afraid the people would dislike it; therefore they adopted a middle-of-the-road policy, prohibited buying on Sundays and in the evenings. That smelt
The War

Mr. Neill

very strongly of discrimination, because we all know the rich man does not generally travel on Sundays. Sunday is the poor man's only opportunity of driving out with his family. It resulted in a few careless people being caught away from home without gasoline, but they soon learned to stock up on Saturday. Meantime it meant in some cases using more gasoline, because if a man got stuck ten miles from home he could not have gasoline sent out to him; he had to get a towing car sent out to bring him home, which meant a double trip and the use of more gasoline than if he had been allowed, perhaps on payment of an extra fee, to get an emergency supply.
There was no give and take whatever. I took it up with officials of the board in my district where men were working in a war production plant or a plant producing a product needed in the war. Naturally they wanted to go home Saturday nights, because there was not enough accommodation at the plant. They had to go about fifteen miles by water, did not get home until late Saturday night, and had to leave Sunday afternoon, consequently they could not get any gasoline at all. I suggested they might be allowed to get gasoline after hours on Saturday and Sunday, but I was told it could not be done, and the suggestions made to meet the situation were absolutely ridiculous. There was no provision to deal reasonably with an emergency.
Then the government, finding that policy was not successful, tried rationing the gasoline stations. As the minister himself said, this was at best a crude method. The obligation to restrict the sale of gasoline fell on the retailer. What would hon. members expect him to do? To say to the rich customer who wanted five gallons: "No, I will give you only two?" Then he would come back the next day and get more. Or was he to say to the rich man: "I will not give you any; I am going to keep it for this poor man who has to drive miles to work?" Where I live men, club together to drive ten miles to work; they cannot get accommodation where they work and they fill a car. One hon. member said he went to a gas station and was told the quota for the day was exhausted. But where I live they did not take that attitude. They said: "We are not going to make bad friends all round; we are going to sell gasoline to everyone who comes while we have it, and if towards the end of the month, say the 25th or 27th, there is none left, we will simply put up notices, "No More Gas." But what about a traveller or the head of a business, who is stuck fifty miles from the nearest town? What is he to do? He would have to send for a towing truck; would that save gasoline? Or

what about these men going to work; were they to remain idle three or four days at the end of the month? I have known of times when these "no gas" notices were up three or four days at the end of the month.
I took this up also, and was told I should appeal to their loyalty. I suggested that was an insult. People have no objection to gasoline restrictions; I have not heard one man object to the restriction, but everyone I spoke to objected to the foolish way in which it was done. That was the point. Provided the method was effective and universal everyone would have been satisfied. Some official told me that we must remember that a very considerable cost will be involved in printing these ration books. There is no doubt this would cost a good deal, but I remember January a year ago when a great deal of money was spent to bring four hundred people here for a three-hour session of parliament, after which we were sent home and an election was brought on, at enormous expense, though at that time it was not immediately essential. So that I do not think the question of expense should be considered so important.
This thing has been dragging on for fifteen months. It will be eighteen months before we are through with it. Until now we have had very little success, but at long last we are going to adopt the principle of compulsion, or should I use that dreadful and fateful word, "conscription", in the matter of gasoline. At last we are going to do something, and the government will find that the people will accept it if the scheme is effective and if it applies to all. The government can trust the people if they tell the absolute facts. Let me quote this sentence, without for the moment giving its source:
The people are not afraid of strong, effective, action-they want action. Listen to discussion in any public place in Canada to-day about the gasoline restrictions. People shrug their shoulders and say, "Well, if it is necessary, I suppose rve must have it." Then, in a burst of exasperation, they usually add, " But if rationing is necessary, in heaven's name why don't we have it without all this pussy-footing?" One minister of the crown says that the situation is "very, very serious." And on the street one hears, "All right, if it's as serious as that why don't they ration us: What are we waiting for?"
That does not come from the journal of the chamber of commerce, or anything like that; it is from the publication of a very prominent labour organization in Canada. That is the way they look at it.
I hope the rules governing this rationing, when they are made, will be just, and without too much red tape; and I hope provision will be made for prompt action in any real emergency. There is no such provision now.

The War-Mr. Neill
To-day if you need an emergency ration you have to communicate with Ottawa, which in my case is three thousand miles away. A woman waiting to go to a maternity hospital, or a man with a broken hip, has not time to communicate with Ottawa, particularly in view of the fact that if the emergency arises on a Saturday afternoon, no answer could be obtained until Monday or Tuesday. I hope there will be some local provision made to meet emergencies of this kind, perhaps through the chief of police or the local magistrate. These are responsible people, who would not abuse their power.
I also hope that local conditions will be taken into consideration when the actual rationing is put into effect; and above all I hope the government will remember that in British Columbia distances are much greater than in the thickly settled regions of the east, and make provision accordingly. And let the arrangements be made for some definite period, not just for a day, a week, or a month. At certain intervals I have occasion to take a trip of some two hundred miles. If I am limited to only a couple of gallons per day I cannot take that trip, but if I am rationed over some length of time I can arrange to save my gasoline when I know this trip has to be made.
There is one other point I should like to mention to the minister. I do not expect an answer at the moment, but perhaps he would be good enough to look into the matter and advise me later. Has he explored the possibility of using charcoal? I understand this has been tried in Australia, and I believe the cost of converting a car to use charcoal is not very considerable. The only trouble seems to be in making provision for stations to provide charcoal at suitable intervals. There is one other matter I should like to bring to his attention also. Australia has made a very full investigation of the possibility of producing alcohol from the refuse of sugar, molasses, wheat, and I think potatoes. They have found that they can produce an alcohol which can be mixed with ordinary gasoline in the ratio of twelve and a half gallons to twenty; and while the resulting mixture is a little more expensive than ordinary gasoline- and gasoline is very expensive in Australia anyway-they are going ahead with the proposition on a very considerable scale. We might be able to do something of the sort here.
There is another matter I wish to discuss, and I hope I will not be called to order. The hon. member for Parkdale was allowed to discuss it last Friday, and if he can discuss it surely I can discuss it also.

Before the hon. member
leaves the subject of rationing, may I ask this question; would not the arguments which he has advanced so splendidly, and with which I entirely agree, apply with equal force to the present method of securing recruits?

them, too?

That this meeting of . . . citizens, having heard read the proclamation of the Hon. Mr. Ralston, Minister of Defence, do entirely endorse and support the appeal made for increased recruiting, but we are of the opinion that the needs of Canada and of the British empire today call for conscription of men and of money, and for control of industry.

The War-Mr. Neill

There is another small percentage who will go only if they are forced to go. Then there is the huge majority who are anxious and willing to go but who will not go unless it is made universal, and I agree with them. Why should they go and make Canada safe for some foreigners who are taking their jobs while they are away? If paying taxes were made optional I would not pay a cent. I pay taxes now because I know it is universal, and everyone is treated in the same way. Increase taxes if necessary; I will not object. Have forced loans if necessary, as was proposed in Australia; they will apply to all. After all, what does conscription mean? It means that we must all do our best, according to our ability, for the common good. That is loyalty; that is democracy; that is necessity and above all it is plain common sense. It is not patriotism; it is common sense, because if Germany wins what are our bonds or properties worth? If Germany wins we will not talk about liberties, because the liberties will be non-existent. Universal service will take many men out of jobs that could be handled by women; and government control, if it took active, vigorous steps, could release many more men.
Go round this town-it is a comparatively small one-and count the number of milk routes. Count how many milk men go into any one apartment house. There may be fifteen or more, when one would do the work equally well-and a great deal cheaper. Look at the delivery trucks operated by gasoline and driven by men-sometimes two men- which have to go a quarter of a mile to deliver a pound of butter to some careless housewife who did not think of getting butter until an hour before meal time.
All these things could be applied to release an enormous number of men for service, universal service-I do not say overseas service, necessarily, because many men are needed in industry. There is universal service in England, Australia, New Zealand and the United States, but not in Canada. Why not? The anti-British element in the United States, the Lindberghs, are taking advantage of the situation, and are pointing out that while they are being conscripted Canadians are not.
At present we have in Canada a large standing army in training-standing looking at each other. If the service were universal they would be satisfied to go where they are most needed. A moment ago I quoted from a labour paper, and I shall quote from it again.

The writer was speaking about gasoline, and asked what we were waiting for. Then he wrote this further sentence, which will be appreciated by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce):
With conscription it is the same; the people are prepared to go twice as far and three times as fast as their government has up to now demanded.
This is published by organized labour. I quote again:
The question of conscription involves the larger and much more vital one of using all our resources to the best advantage.
"All our resources"-men, machinery and so on. Then again:
.We want to survive as a people. We are fighting this war to be able to settle our own affairs in our own way, we and our children after us. We are willing to pay the price- any price. Why are our leaders afraid to ask the price that we, the people, are willing to pay? Let us have conscription by all means: all-out conscription for an all-out effort. . . . We want conscription of men for war; and we want them to have the tools to work with. We want conscription of those tools along with the men. We do not see why the tools should be exempted when our boys are taken.
As I say, this is not alone the opinion of some soldiers' body; or of big industrial concerns; it is the opinion also of the working people of Canada who are in organized labour. They so express themselves. If this rule-it was not a rule, but rather an ultimatum-by which we talk, but may not move anything in this committee, had not been enforced, I would have moved a resolution to test the feeling of the house. But as it is being enforced, the hon. member for Parkdale and myself will have to be content- very poorly content-by simply expressing our views in the matter. I suppose we will have to leave it to a larger parliament, a larger expression of the people. It is regrettable however that in a matter of so much importance we should not be allowed to take action. It is idle to suggest that it is not a prominent and vital question today in Canada. Go to any street corner, or to any place where a body of people is meeting, and we find that the question is discussed. They are ready for an all-out effort, and an all-out effort can be obtained only by universal conscription of us all-as this article said, of us all-working for the common good.

The War-Mr. Pouliot
Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Terais-eouata):	Mr. Chairman, it seems that as a
basis for the discussion of this important problem we should consider the three Canadian acts of parliament concerning conscription.
First there is the Militia Act, chapter 132 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927. Section 64 of that act reads:
The governor in council may place the militia, or any part thereof, on active service anywhere in Canada, and also beyond Canada, for the defence thereof, at any time when it appears advisable so to do by reason of emergency.
This is the Cartier act, which was amended by Sir Wilfrid Laurier after the Transvaal war by adding the words "for the defence thereof" in the third line.
Since then the only amendment to the act, although the present act does not specifically mention the Militia Act, is chapter 21 of the Statutes of Canada for 1932-33, the title of which reads as follows:
An act to make provision with respect to forces of his majesty from other parts of the British commonwealth or from a colony when visiting the Dominion of Canada; and with respect to the exercise of command and discipline when forces of his majesty from different parts of the commonwealth are serving together; and with respect to the attachment of members of one such force to another such force, and with respect to deserters from such forces.
This act was passed when Mr. Bennett was in power, and was given royal assent on April 12, 1933.
The second conscription act, known as the Military Service Act, 1917, was passed by the Borden government. The purpose of that act is approximately the same as that of the preceding one, with the exception of an inversion of phraseology respecting the aim or purpose of the act.
Then, the third conscription act is the National Resources Mobilization Act, 1940, assented to on June 21, 1940. Section 2 of that act is as follows:
Subject to the provisions of section 3 hereof, the governor in council may do and authorize such acts and things, and make from time to time such orders and regulations, requiring persons to place themselves, their services and their property at the disposal of his majesty in the right of Canada, as may be deemed necessary or expedient for securing the public safety, the defence of Canada, the maintenance of public order, or the efficient prosecution of the war, or for maintaining supplies or services essential to the life of the community.
Then, section 3 states:
The powers conferred by the next preceding section may not be exercised for the purpose of requiring persons to serve in the military, naval or air forces outside of Canada and the territorial waters thereof.
The marginal note for section 3 reads: "Limitation in respect of service overseas."
When the resolution preceding the bill from which this act followed was submitted to the house I remember well that the leader of the opposition then said it constituted one of his suggestions which had been adopted; therefore at the time he was satisfied with the legislation, and believed that it was a step forward.
I am not quoting him verbatim, but I believe that is the effect of what he said.
It would seem therefore that there are three conscription acts on the statute books of Canada. The first two, namely, the Cartier act, as amended by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and the Borden act, are altogether different from the one passed last year for the defence of Canada. That is evidently the reason why the mobilization act was passed. The aim and purpose of that act is the defence of Canada, and everyone agrees with that principle.
There is another feature which must be considered, namely the exemptions which appear in each of the acts. Section 9 of the Militia Act enumerates the following exemptions:
9. The following persons only shall be exempt from liability from service in the militia:-
Members of the King's Privy Council for Canada;
Judges of all courts of justice;
Members of the executive councils of provinces;
Deputy ministers of the federal and provincial governments;
Clergy and ministers of all religious denominations;
Telegraph clerks in actual employment;
Officers and clerks regularly employed in the collection of the revenue;
Wardens and officers of all public prisons and lunatic asylums;
Members of the naval militia;
Members of the police force and fire brigade permanently employed in incorporated cities, towns and villages;
Professors in colleges and universities, and teachers in religious orders;
Persons disabled by bodily or mental infirmity;
The only son of a widow, being her only support;
Pilots and apprentice pilots during the season of navigation;
Persons who, from the doctrines of their religion, are averse to bearing arms or rendering personal military service, under such conditions as are prescribed.
That last exemption I find absurd.
But there is something else, which I find in section 24, subsection 2, which reads:
If there are inscribed on the militia roll more than one son belonging to the same family residing in the same house, only one of such sons shall be drawn, unless the number of names so inscribed is insufficient to complete the required proportion of service men.

That is the Borden law, and I object to paragraph (f) just cited for the same reason that I objected to the last exemption provided by section 9 of the Militia Act. I do not believe that Doukhobors, Mennonites and 
conscientious objectors should enjoy exemption from military service. This may be the feeling also of quite a number of members, although I do not speak for them; I am speaking for myself alone.
The main difference between the mobilization act of 1940 and the two previous acts which I have cited is that there is no provision in the mobilization act of 1940 for exemption, but a free hand is given to the governor in council to pass regulations enumerating possible exemptions. Parliament did not legislate upon these exemptions, which by virtue of the act itself were to be framed by the governor in council. What are the exemptions provided by virtue of the regulations that were passed by order in council some time after this house was adjourned and when there were very few members of parliament in this city? Section 6 of the National War Services Regulations, 1940 (Recruits) provides:
The following persons shall be excepted from being called out:-
(a)	Judges of superior, district or county courts of justice;
(b)	Members of the clergy or religious orders;
(c)	Regular clergymen or ministers of religious denominations;
(d)	Members of the naval, military or air forces of Canada on active service and cadets entered at the Royal Military College of Canada;

Those are the only exemptions. The exemptions provided for by the Borden act are not mentioned in these regulations. They were completely set aside.
There is another exemption, although it is not mentioned in section 6 of the regulations, and that is that when a man is suffering from ill-health or is unfit for service he may be put in a class where he will not have to serve or will serve only in this country.
There are four classes of exemptions provided in the regulations against which I strongly protest. Three of them are not mentioned exactly as exemptions but are spoken of as adjournments. The first exemption is not even mentioned as an adjournment. But the phraseology of the regulations gives a certain advantage to a certain class of British citizens who have not to comply with the regulations as every Canadian-born or Canadian-domiciled citizen must do. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) said rightly, speaking in March and again in September, 1939, that a British citizen

enjoyed the same rights in England as in Canada. I have a French translation of his remarks here, but I will give in English the substance of his remarks. He said that we have the same national status as England; a British subject in Canada is also a British subject in London and anywhere else in the British commonwealth, and a British subject in England is also a British subject in Canada. It means that all young English babies, blonde and beautiful, of military age, twenty years old and over, who come to Canada are not supposed in virtue of these regulations to get into military service. Apparently it means that it would be bad manners to enlist them as conscripts, as draftees; and they may come here-I do not speak of guest children, I refer to those of military age-they may come to this haven of security, Canada, those who are British citizens and to whom these regulations should apply, and they can get any jobs because they are not ordinarily residents of Canada; they are here only "for the duration." They can take the jobs that the young boys who are domiciled in Canada have to leave when the time of enlistment comes. A young man who is born in Canada and who does useful work here has to get into the army, while a young Englishman who is fortunate enough to find passage on a clipper or boat and come here has no trouble at all. It is well known what happened in Montreal in a store not long ago, when an aged mother who had two sons in the army, one of whom is now missing, was served by a young "bloke": she asked him where he had come from, and he said, "I have come from England, and I have fine connections." She threw her parcel in his face and left the store, very indignant. I do not know why we do things like that. If we are all British citizens we should be under the same law, and there should be no exception for those of military age who come here from the British isles for the duration of the war. That is my first point.
And a very weak one.

My second point is that there should be no exemption for Mennonites and Doukhobors. They came here some years ago and were granted privileges through orders in council passed in the time of Sir John A. Macdonald and Sir Wilfrid Laurier. But there was then no thought of a war like this. When we speak about the difficulties that some
people may have, we are answered that these are not ordinary times. The fourth class of exemptions against which I protest veiy strongly is that of conscientious objectors. I do not see why a man should be exempted just because he says-, "My conscience forbids me to abide by the law." It is one of the absurdities of the English legislation as well as of the Canadian legislation. Why should a man have the right to defy the law in such a fashion? I wonder if there is a single hon. member of this committee who would seriously say that, because England has given that privilege to conscientious objectors, we should give it to them here. There is another thing that I cannot understand. It is that, in virtue of the first draft of the regulations which I am discussing, Doukhobors, Mennonites, and conscientious objectors were entitled to an indefinite postponement of their draft; and now the word "indefinite" is left out; but they enjoy the indefinite postponement just the same. As a consequence, if a man is a Doukhobor, a Mennonite, or a conscientious objector, he will not serve in the army for the whole time of the war. Is it fair? No sir, it is not fair.

It is that, for that privilege, that exemption-I call it an exemption because it can be given by only one of the commissioners-for Canadian-born citizens who are neither Doukhobors, Mennonites, conscientious objectors, or the Canadian who is not a "bloke", a quorum of two commissioners of the three is required for a short postponement not exceeding six months. It is unfair that Mennonites and Doukhobors are exempted, not because they are good farmers-it has to be proved that they are good farmers-not in the public interest, but just because they are sectarian. But do you not think that there is discrimination in provisions like that?

These occupations are no longer referred to as seasonal occupations; they are mentioned as seasonal and essential occupations. Subsections 1 and
2	read:
(1) When considering any application made in accordance with section 10 hereof, the board before which the application is made shall have power to grant an advancement or postpone-

The War-Mr. Ross (Souris)
ment order when it is of the opinion that it is in the national interest to do so and, in granting such order, the board shall state the reasons for such opinion. No postponement order may be made for more than six months, but, upon reviewing the application, the board may grant one or more extensions; provided that the board may cancel the order at any time for military reasons or for cause: Provided further that there shall be no exemption and no indefinite postponement of military training or service.
(2) When considering an application for postponement order by a man engaged in farming, fishing, lumbering, trapping, mining, placer mining, gold prospecting, seafaring, railroad transportation, public utility, or engaged in an occupation which the minister has declared to be a seasonal occupation or one essential to the successful prosecution of the war or in the national interest, the board shall take into account the supply of labour available, and the importance of the particular applicant's occupation to the national economy.
This is important, because what I understand by conscription is mobilization as defined by the Prime Minister and by members of the cabinet when the bill was before the house last year. It means total war, a total war effort; that is to say, that each one who makes an effort that serves the country best should be in the right place to make that effort, And nobody should have any objection to it, provided that the necessary distinctions are made in due course. What I complain of bitterly is the kind of propaganda that we have from the information bureau. There is one kind for English-speaking Canadians and another and altogether different kind for the French-Canadians of Quebec. I cannot understand it. We are all Canadians. I am not strong for the word "unity"; I rather think the word "union" is better. It means union of souls, union of human beings, union of minds for a common purpose, but "unity" is used of .inanimate things. As it is accepted now and as we speak of national unity, national unity would be much better served if there wrnre no Chinese wall around the province of Quebec in regard to propaganda. I fully agree with what was said by the hon. member for Broadview last Friday; it would be much better to dispense with such propaganda.
I am not a communist and I take the Russian propaganda with a grain of salt. Nevertheless the propaganda we have just received from Russia about fascism is the best propaganda I have ever read since the beginning of the war. It puts us to shame that the Russians are writing better war propaganda than our information bureau. I would like that bureau to be abolished. My idea would be to have all speeches delivered in both languages, and for those who cannot
speak one of the official languages of the country a translation of the speech should be given on the French network at the same time the talk is given over the English network.
Why not broadcast the speeches of the house?

I regret I did not hear the hon. member.
The ACTING CHAIRMAN (Mr. Bradette); I have to inform the hon. member that he has spoken for forty minutes.

Like many others, having come to Ottawa after four and a half months' adjournment I am very much disappointed with the speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in which he did not mention Canada or our war effort at all. We are certainly being reduced to government by order in council; in fact parliament has been reduced to a sounding board for the government. Last spring a committee on war expenditures was set up. A very grave charge was made by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Maybank) with reference to the heating plant in a cordite factory there. The minister said the place to make these charges was before that committee. But the terms of reference wrere not broad enough for the committee to consider the matter. The hon. member charged that this heating equipment would result in a waste of $200,000 a year, yet the question could not be investigated by the committee. That makes the committee a complete farce in the minds of the people of this country.
Referring to gasoline, it is evident that little thought was given to the agricultural population of western Canada when that order in council was passed. Imagine in harvest time the people of western Canada, to whom the former speaker referred as mechanical producers, having to stop their harvesting operations on a sunny afternoon in order to go to the nearest trading centre to obtain gasoline. Surely that was not in the interest of the national effort, to say nothing of the hardship to the individual.
In connection with gasoline I have received a letter from a man at Castlegar, British Columbia, in which he said:
With the new gasoline restrictions in effect it has brought to my mind the fact that the Toronto Star Weekly several months back ran a series of articles on a carburettor that was capable of delivering up to three hundred miles to the gallon of gasoline. This carburettor, invented by a Winnipeg man, according to the Star was proved out on a run from Winnipeg to Vancouver and was very successful. As I understand it the rights to this carburettor we.re
The War-Mr. Rass (Souris)

purchased by some large oil company and retired from the public eye, to the financial interest of the oil company concerned.
My idea is that if the present administration was to introduce legislation compelling individuals or companies who hold patent rights on inventions that can be used to the advantage of Canada, to release these rights to the country for whatever remuneration a board of arbitration should decide.
In the case of the above mentioned carburettor, it would make the present gasoline restrictions unnecessary, or if it was used only on our war machines it would be a wonderful contribution to our war effort. Don't you think so?
I know something of a carburettor invented in Winnipeg by a Mr. Pogue. I witnessed some of the experiments there. I do not know what became of it, but rumours were rife that some large oil company had bought it. I trust the minister will look into that for the benefit of this committee.
Like the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) I am sorry that we have not the opportunity to move resolutions in this committee. Certainly our efforts have been very much circumscribed. The discussion of national selective service would be timely, and I cannot understand the Prime Minister's interpretation a little while ago that discussion must be confined to one department, because certainly the Minister of Munitions and Supply, the Minister of Agriculture and the ministers of national defence are vitally concerned in this matter and should be working together in close coordination.
I was elected as opposed to conscription, but I was careful at that time to point to my experience in the last war and to say that if the unexpected happened we should then give the matter further consideration. I do not think there is any hon. member who will not admit that the unexpected has happened since March, 1910, with the fall of France and many other countries.
We have heard much about an all-out war effort, but I venture to say that not fifty per cent, probably not over thirty-five per cent of our possibilities are being exerted in an all-out war effort.
I believe there is a great deal of misunderstanding of what national selective service means. It is not a matter of taking all the men off the farms. Many men who have enlisted from the farms would under this scheme be left on the farms where they properly should be. Key executive men have been taken from industry who should have been left there. I doubt whether many of us appreciate the brief placed before the government by the

Canadian Legion. I should like to refer to an article which appeared in the Winnipeg
Tribune:
The Canadian Legion and Man-Power
Attempts have been made to show that proponents of an all-out war programme for Canada want to conscript vast numbers of soldiers at the expense of Canada's industrial effort. This is nonsense. ...
In particular, the Canadian Legion does not propose mobilization of Canadian man-power simply to increase the armed forces. It demands, rather, that mobilization of man-power should be undertaken immediately in order that our resources of man-power may be used for our needs, whether in the field of agriculture or industry or in the fighting services.
Here is the main plank in the legion's call for "total war". It takes the form of a statement presented to Prime Minister King by the dominion executive of the legion on October 21, calling upon the Prime Minister to institute all necessary measures to place Canada on a total war footing. The legion specifically said:
By "total war" the legion means:
(a)	Immediate, complete and scientific mobilization, organization and utilization of all our resources-spiritual, intellectual, natural, financial, agricultural, industrial, man-power-in such manner that Canada may be geared to produce essential foods and munitions and to wage war to her maximum capacity.
(b)	The services of all men and women to be employed to the best and most useful effect, according to the age, training, physical capacity and ability of the individual;
(c)	By an intelligent extension of the principles contained in the National Resources Mobilization Act and by the elimination of the provisions restricting service to Canada only-our armed forces in Canada and overseas, including reserves and reinforcements, to be maintained at the highest possible strength, consistent with our industrial and other requirements;
(d)	An equitable division of the burden of service, sacrifice, contribution and effort among all our people to be the basic principle underlying this "total war" policy;
(e)	The cumulative results of this "total effort" to be devoted to the single purpose of destroying the enemy.
That is a reasonable programme. It is also one which the public of Canada at large can support.
As The Tribune has said, again and again, the issue ... is the issue of mobilizing all our man-power-not simply a matter of sending men overseas. The Legion clearly recognizes this. The public feels it instinctively and is coming to recognize it more and more clearly*. The chief laggard is the dominion government which still refuses to face certain realities that the man in the street has long accepted.
There was some difference of opinion between our various ministers of defence the other day; but I was very sorry to see the presentation of the Minister of National Defence made the subject matter of an editorial in the Ottawa Journal of November 7, headed: "Mr. Ralston's Proud Speech; Mr. NOVEMBER 10, 1941
The War-Mr. MacNicol
Ralston's False Speech." Those of us who are returned men have a very great respect for the Minister of National Defence as a fine soldier. This editorial goes on to state that the minister was not speaking his own mind, that it was a matter of cabinet solidarity. At this time, after all that has happened, as one soldier to another might I suggest that he shake off the cloak of political expediency and cabinet solidarity, and really face the critical national situation in which we find ourselves. This is not a matter that affects his department alone. He made the suggestion that some consideration was given to industry in connection with men enlisting in the army. The minister for air, who followed him, said he did not agree with that statement, that he made no exemptions whatever but took holus-bolus all those who offered their services.
I believe the situation overseas is much more critical than many people throughout Canada realize. I am sure everyone who has gone overseas, who has had free access to industrial centres throughout the British isles, who has spoken off the record with that great inspirational leader, Mr. Churchill, agrees that the situation is so critical that it should not be made a matter of political expediency at this time. We are all vitally concerned with this matter, and I am sure we have all received wires and letters during the last few days from many of the most outstanding organizations in the country, from town councils, rural municipalities, boards of trade, the Canadian Legion, all urging this government to take some action before the end of this session of parliament. Certainly the step we are urging is most timely, and I think will be supported by all the citizens of Canada once they properly understand it. I know many young men who feel they should be in the armed forces but who make the plain statement that if this government has not the courage of its convictions, why should they offer their services. These men reason that the government knows more about the situation than they know; and, while I cannot give you the exact phrases they use, they say if the members of the government are prepared to do what is required of them, in the office they hold, then the young men are prepared to make any sacrifice that may be necessary.
I hope therefore that due consideration will be given by the government at once to instituting national selective service at this time, in the interests of people in all walks of life; for I am sure many ministers realize what their duty requires of them in the present situation.

Mr. Chairman, together with all other hon. members I listened carefully as the ministers made their reports; and those I did not hear I have read. While in the main they give a very good story of what Canada is trying to do, I am sorry to say that we have no yardstick with which to measure what we are attempting as compared with what is being done in other parts of the empire, in order that we may convince ourselves that we are doing our fair share. Certainly the general public throughout Canada are convinced that we are not doing our share. I cannot say whether or not we are, unless I compare our efforts with those of other parts of the empire.
I listened attentively to the report of the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe). He is the one man in the cabinet, I believe, wrho really knows-I should not say anything-very much about manufacturing, and he tells a very good story of what is being done in the manufacturing plants of Canada. I should like to refer briefly to some things I have observed myself; for I, too, have visited perhaps fifty to seventy-five of the large plants of this country. I need refer only to one or two items to which the minister also referred. He spoke about guns and shells. As Canadians I believe we should be proud of what has been done by certain manufacturers in this country in the production of lathes to make shells. I am told that the John T. Hepburn company of Toronto, which now employs about- four thousand men in several plants, has produced lathes which are now used in the manufacture of more than half the shells used on the British side. I have frequently seen ten to fifteen carloads of these great lathes being shipped to Australia, south Africa, India, Egypt and elsewhere. As a Canadian I am proud that such a genius as John Hepburn is a resident of this country during this great war. I know he has received commendation from the British government; I do not know wffiether he has received any commendation from the Canadian government. Recently he produced what is said to be the first satisfactory lathe in the world capable of drilling gun barrels from both ends at the same time, which enables these gun barrels to be produced in much less time than is required in other plants throughout the world. These lathes are now being produced in quantity and are being supplied to Canadian companies making various sizes of gun barrels.
The minister also said something about tanks and ships. I think he should have given the official opposition some credit for spurring
The War-Mr. MacNicol

the government into the production of tanks in this country. I remember that when the subject was under discussion a year ago, as one who was connected with steel and iron manufacturing for many years I said this country could produce every component part required in the production of tanks. We can do what the Australians can do. They have produced tank manufacturing plants. Not only that, they have had to produce their own tools with which to make their tanks. On the other hand Canada had to the south of it a great republic from which to purchase machine tools, and could obtain a supply in addition to the vast number we make ourselves.
Whether the minister gave credit or not, as a member of the official opposition I am going to take some credit to that group for the fact that we are now producing tanks, guns and steel ships in Canada. In doing that I do not detract from the minister, nor do I suggest that he has not exercised his best efforts to see that these things are being done. My only point is that the official opposition had a good deal to say about each of those products before they were made in Canada.
I am going to speak briefly concerning what was said by each of the ministers, because I do not expect to be here to-morrow or the next day. For that reason, if I may be permitted I should like to make a statement at this time. Some observations have been made respecting labour. Having been connected with labour for at least a quarter of a century, I do not yield to any member of the house, no matter what his party may be, or no matter where he comes from, in my loyalty to labour and its rights. I, myself, was a labour man-not with my tongue but with my hands and head.
I was disappointed in the report of a recent speech by the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) as it was reported in the Toronto Globe and Mail of October 8, 1941. The minister is reported as follows:
Speaking of labour Mr. Crerar said there is a widespread feeling in Canada that responsible Canadian labour leaders failed in leadership.
The responsible labour leaders I know are Tom Moore, A. R. Mosher, R. Y. Menary, Raoul Trepanier, John Kelly and John Noble. These are outstanding labour leaders, and I have not read anywhere that those leaders have done anything less than their utmost to maintain order in the unions throughout Canada. There may be the odd one who could be placed in the class referred to by the minister, but he would not be as outstanding as the men whose names I have mentioned.
It is the government that has failed.
Well-
The hon. member need not agree.

I am only commenting on a statement made by the Minister of Mines and Resources. Perhaps he did not mean to make it-I have said things which I would have withdrawn, had I been given the chance. I try, however, to be as careful as I can.
I worked at arduous labour for many years, and stated long ago the rights to which I believed labour was entitled. I am conversant with what this country undertook when it signed the treaty of Versailles, which is now "washed up". Nevertheless, the labour articles adopted under the Versailles treaty were good. Their principles were, in brief, (a) that labour should not be regarded as a commodity or article of commerce, and (b) that there should be a right enjoyed by employers and employees to set up associations.
I believe that those are proper principles, and I cannot for the life of me understand why those associations, under proper guidance, could not sit down and iron out their disputes. Both employers and employees have rights. Many people take objection to the term "collective bargaining", but I do not look upon the procedure as one of collective bargaining. Rather, I consider it collective representation. If sincere men representing labour and sincere men representing industry sit down round a common table, as is taking place all across this country to-day in many shops where disputes have arisen, I believe many of our troubles could be ironed out. In my opinion it is the duty of the government to wash out those troubles.
Without casting any reflection on any member of the cabinet, I cannot help thinking that if in Canada we had a. minister of labour like Bevin in England, a man since the beginning of his life seized with the rights of labour, we would be able to iron out our difficulties in a more satisfactory manner.
It will be understood that in what I say I am not singling out that estimable gentleman who is at present responsible for the Department of Labour. I am pleased that the department has seen fit to employ a man who formerly sat in the house. I refer to Mr. Humphrey Mitchell. I met Mr. Mitchell in different places across Canada during the past summer, when he was engaged in the adjustment of labour disputes. When I met him last, in the city of Winnipeg, he and others associated with him were successful in

The War-Mr. MacNicol
bringing about a settlement. I would expect that of Mr. Mitchell, because he has been a labour man-and I do not refer to "labour" in the political sense. I am referring to Mr. Mitchell as a worker, one who has worked hard all through his life. As a matter of fact, I believe he was in a line of business similar to that in which I was engaged.
During the past summer I made some investigations in respect of plants where they were having trouble. I am convinced that in some of the plants in Toronto in which there have been strikes the cause can be traced to the government's own plant in that city. In Toronto the government has a large plant employing several thousands. I believe the employees in that plant are treated exceptionally well. I am informed that cost of production in the government plant is not all important, because the operators receive a certain percentage above costs. On the other hand a private plant cannot operate on that basis. It has not the government behind it to guarantee that there will be no loss. It must sharpen its pencil, and figure out costs. Government plants do not have to do that. While I am in heart}- accord with the government's setting an example of good wages, reasonable hours, and so on, it must be understood that every other plant cannot operate on the same basis.
Therefore, if the government intends to prevent strikes in other plants which cannot operate in a similar manner, certainly it should tiy to prevent strikes by providing a sufficiently large cost of living bonus for the men and women working in private plants. I am strongly in favour of adequate return for adequate service. If privately owned companies could operate on the same basis as government plants, they would be able to do what those government plants are now doing.
Something has been said about oil. I am not going to speak at length at this time on that subject, but I purpose doing so at the next session. On that occasion, after travel during the summer which extended over fifteen thousand miles, I intend to set out a programme of national rehabilitation. I should like, however, to make one or two observations in advance about oil. The minister presented the problem clearly. I cannot forget one salient circumstance, namely that several million German soldiers are hastening as fast as they can toward the Caucasus, the Russian oil fields, principally centred round Batum. In that area about
218,000,000 barrels are produced each year. If the Caucasus are taken, what is to stop the Germans from taking Iraq and Iran, where
about 80,000,000 to 100,000,000 barrels are produced? They already have the Rumanian fields, where about 40,000,000 barrels are produced. If they were successful in obtaining the three other fields I have mentioned, they would have all the oil required to fight a wrar for any length of time they might wish to fight it.
The largest producer of oil is the United States, which produces more than all other countries of the world put together. The United States produces 1,350,000,000 barrels of oil a year. Canada produces just a little over
8,000,000 barrels a year. I remember, before the war broke out, hearing or reading, or both, that the German government or someone associated with it had applied to Canada-I do not remember how-for the right to run a pipeline from an oil field in Canada to the Pacific coast. I cannot think for one second that they had the Turner valley oil field in mind. The Turner valley is a really fine oil field, well managed and with an excellent plant, as good as any in the world. I was through it and was greatly pleased with what I saw. But its capacity is limited. I remember last session asking the Minister of Mines and Resources if it would be worth while running a pipeline from Turner valley to the Pacific coast, and as I remember, he replied in the negative. Then what part of the country did Hitler or the German government have in mind to run a pipeline from? After a thorough investigation I am convinced that what they had in mind was running a pipeline from the Athabaska river near McMurray at the junction of the Athabaska and Clearwater rivers.
I am quite aware of the fact that there can be an improvement in the method of extracting oil from the oil sands. I also know that the McMurray oil fields are not too far away to run a pipeline from there to Edmonton. On the Athabaska river we have by far the greatest potential oil field in the world. It is said that Canada could produce from there one hundred billion barrels of oil, and United States geologists have put the figure at two hundred and fifty billion barrels of potential oil. There can be improvements made in extraction, although they are doing a very satisfactory job there now. They are producing and shipping oil-I saw it at various mines-seven or eight hundred miles north, and I heard it pronounced as good as the best in the world. If those statements are true, and I know that they are true, and that they are producing oil and doing it fairly rapidly-it takes only three minutes to extract the oil, twenty minutes to get it into the tanks, and seventy minutes to turn it into
The War-Mr. MacNicol

finished oil; it is said the system of extraction can be improved-therefore I am going to ask the minister between now and the next session of parliament to have his department investigate the possibilities in that region. Oil is perhaps the most important of our munitions requirements, and next year we may have to be shipping vast quantities of oil for the use of the British navy; for it may be-I hope it will not be-impossible for them to get the oil from Iraq or Iran, and there is no other source except the Dutch East Indies, which produces only about sixty million barrels a year; Venezuela, which produces about two hundred million barrels a year, and the United States. Therefore I am going to ask the minister to have his engineers survey that oil field, and if it is found that vast quantities of oil can be produced rapidly, to bring a bill into this house, if necessary, to erect refineries, or support companies that will do it, in the Athabaska river valley or the Peace river valley, for they have a lot of oil there too, with a view to our producing the greatest possible quantity of oil. I quite realize that to do so might result in our having too many refineries after the war. But that is not our problem now. Our problem to-day is to win the war, and then deal with these other problems after the war. If the minister with his energy will undertake to have that field surveyed and the possibilities explored, I hope that he will have something to present to the house next session, when I propose to deal with this question in a much more extended way.
I wish to speak for a moment about maintaining harmony in industry. The government has granted a cost of living bonus-and I am heartily in accord with that step-to certain classes of the civil service which it believes should be granted such a bonus. Certain municipalities have done likewise, also some industrial plants. I hope that some method may be worked out whereby all workers in industry will be granted a cost of living bonus.
I should like the present scheme to go further, for the sake of maintaining harmony in this country. I should like to see a cost of living bonus granted to pensioned returned soldiers of the last war and to the dependents of soldiers of this war and the great war, and further I should like to see a cost of living bonus granted to those receiving old age pensions. I know that would make a long list, but harmony in war time is essential, and you cannot have harmony if you give a cost of living bonus to this class and that class and leave out other classes. It should be uniform and apply all round.
To the farmers, too?

I certainly believe that the farmers are deserving of consideration and I have always been an advocate for them. In fact, I have come to the conclusion, after travelling extensively in the farming areas of the west, that there are places where the farmers should be given a pension for staying on the farm. They do the very best work, and farming is an essential part of our war effort.
I have made a bit of a survey in our retail stores, and I know that when the average working man's wife goes to a merchant on St. Clair avenue in Toronto, the part of the city where I live, but it applies everywhere else, she finds, as I found when I made investigation, that the cost of what she has to buy has gone up on many commodities from forty to sixty per cent. I know that some classes are receiving a small cost of living bonus, but certainly it is not the equivalent of a forty to sixty per cent rise in the price of the necessaries of life which the average housewife has to pay.
I wish to refer to something the Minister for Naval Services (M. Macdonald) said the other day. He said that submarines had been sighted off the coast of Labrador. Last year when I was making a survey along the shores of Hudson bay I talked at Churchill with some of the old residents there, and they told me that when the Eskimos came to Churchill in the summer they had reported seeing igloos floating on the water with a stovepipe sticking out of the top of the igloo. If the Eskimos really saw an igloo with a smoke pipe, if that was not the product of their imagination, it was not an igloo at all but a submarine. I do not for a moment say that submarines have been in there, but on the other hand I see no reason under the sun why they could not get in there. For a submarine to get into Hudson bay, all it has to do is to come west of Greenland, enter a very deep and wide strait-from forty to a hundred miles wide-pass between a few islands at the mouth of Hudson bay, and then it is in that great bay which is almost an ocean by itself. No one can predict what will have happened by this time next year. I have read that in Germany they are producing very large submarines, which will carry aeroplanes, and I have been saying to myself, what will happen if a submarine gets into Hudson bay carrying high-powered bombing planes and releases them somewhere near the south end of the bay? That, I believe, Mr. Chairman, is in your own bailiwick, or not far from the constituency which you represent. A submarine arrving in Hudson bay might release an aeroplane which could make a round trip of a couple of thousand miles and might blow Winnipeg right off the map; the city would

The War-Mr. MacNicol
have no defence beyond, perhaps, a few antiaircraft guns. At least I do not know; I hope it has a good many. For that matter, perhaps German submarines might send aeroplanes down to Toronto and blow it oil the map; it is not more than 900 to 1,000 miles from the south end of Hudson bay. I hope that the government has provided against events of that kind. I am told that there are aeroplane fields up in that country; I hope there are, and that there is adequate defence of our back-door. But this summer, when I was travelling in that million-square-mile area north of Edmonton, up around the 63rd parallel, I inquired from those who should be informed as to how many mounted policemen were up there, and was told that from the 63rd parallel north there were approximately thirty. I hope there are more than that, in view of the danger from high-powered aeroplanes. Our back-doors in the north are, I trust, properly provided with equipment to shoot off any aeroplanes coming from that direction.
I have just a word or two to say about recruiting. I have travelled a great deal this past summer. I visited various towns where there are military camps, and saw some things which I did not like, and which might be expected under the system under which we are now recruiting men for the army. I was rather alarmed when the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) made the statement the other day that recruiting had fallen down. I noticed that on Friday last the Hon. Charles Dunning, who sat in this chamber for many years, referred to the matter in these words:
This is our war. Waiting for it to come to Montreal is the surest way of letting it reach our shores.
On the same occasion, Brigadier-General Panet mentioned the statement of the Minister of National Defence that recruiting in the past months had dropped. That is a serious circumstance. It is not for me to tell the government how it is going to get recruits; that is their responsibility. But I want strongly to emphasize my belief that the government should tell us before we go home how they expect to get the necessary recruits without some system of national compulsory service. I am not going to tell them the system. There are different systems. I am not familiar with the one in use in the United States, nor can I say that I know how the British system operates; but there is a method whereby governments can get recruits, and it should be selective; the men should not be taken holus-bolus. As an industrialist I realize that there are many good men in tank plants, gun plants, screw plants, and factories making all the components which enter into the construction
of war munitions who should not be taken into the army. Well, how are you going to keep them out of the army unless you have some system of selection? The same consideration applies to agriculture, in the case of farmers' sons and the like. My investigation showed me that there is something which is not quite right. The Minister of National Defence was quite emphatic the other evening as to the government's objective; he said that the government of Canada is pledged to an all-out war effort, and he then stated that that effort at the moment amounted to the following:
At the present time we have overseas-
I assume, in England.

the first and second divisions, the third division which went overseas in July; the army tank brigade, and thousands of corps and army troops,-
To which, he said, he would refer a little later. Then he added:
We have in Canada the fifth armoured division, which according to the programme is to go overseas before very long.
Upon being questioned, he added that the total number of men now overseas is 110,000. I have been trying to read up what is being done by other parts of the empire and to make some deductions therefrom, and I found a statement as to the recent campaigns in Greece and Crete. I have not so far come across a statement about the campaign last winter in Libya. But, regarding the Greek and Cretan campaigns, I find that Australia and New Zealand had, in Greece, 33,657 men and in Crete, some 13,550 troops, or a total of 47,207.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: You did not add the two together, did you?

The troops engaged in Greece and in Crete were partly, but not wholly the same. The Crete totals at the start of the fighting included men evacuated from Greece but not reevacuated to Egypt before the Crete operations. I have not been able to separate the numbers who were taken out of Greece into Crete; certainly not all of them were, because the numbers in Crete were very much smaller than those engaged in Greece. At all events, taking the situation of Greece alone, it is clear that there were 33,657 Australians and New Zealanders, of whom 5,234 were killed, wounded, or missing-captured or otherwise. Then, of the numbers of Australian and New Zealand troops who had been in Greece and went to Crete, plus any others, the loss in Crete was 6,100; a total of 11,334. If you deduct those as casualties from a total of 33.657, the losses amount to approximately thirty-three and a third per cent.
The War-Mr. MacNicol

Let me say here at once that there are no better aviators in the world than the Canadians and I am sure they will give a good account of themselves wherever they go. I will say at once, however, that so far as the Canadian Press is concerned, I believe any dispatch it sends out is correct as far as it has the facts. Now that the recruiting effort has been mentioned, may I make this statement after what the Minister of National Defence said. He told us that there were several committees-the civilian committee, the agriculture committee, the industrial committee-all of them working as best they can to persuade young men working in various plants and on farms to enter the service. Let me tell the committee what I saw in connection with this system.
-NOVEMBER 10, 1941
The War-Mr. Gillis
I travelled a good deal last summer, and one evening I saw in front of a hotel in the west two stout, well built men, far beyond the fighting age-they were as old as I am-bulldozing a young man about joining the army. I did not wish to reveal who I was because I thought I might get into trouble, but I certainly do not agree with that system of recruiting. I do not agree with the bulldozing of young men in the street. I cannot endorse that method of intimidation. Young men have a great responsibility, and if they want to enlist, if it is in their hearts, I assume they will volunteer. That has been the British spirit at all times, but I do not believe in the intimidation of young mem. May I mention what I was told in one recruiting camp. I do not believe this, but I will tell the committee what I heard; I hope it is wholly untrue. At any rate, I heard that three pieces of paper were handed to a young chap and they would ask him to choose the one he wanted, The blue one said that he would enlist; the white one said that he would consider it and think it over; the yellow paper declared that he was not going to enlist for overseas service at all. I hope there is not a word of truth in that, though I have heard it and I believe others have. If it is true, I am not in accord with it.
I am not going to back up the statement about recruiting falling down. I have here a good many clippings from Pembroke, Winnipeg and across Canada. I am going to take the minister's statement in this regard. The state of affairs being what it is, and taking the loss of our troops in wastage, through sickness, through men being sent home for one reason or another, I would ask this question.

The hon. member has referred to Pembroke. Has he read in the newspapers that the enlistments in the Pembroke district to date are equal to the enlistments in that district for the four years of the last war?
How does the population compare?
The population is about what it was.

I am not finding fault with what was done in the Pembroke district. I have no doubt the young men there will enlist as loyally as in any other part of Canada, but I have this statement from the press:
Pembroke, Oct. 17-(staff)-Concern over a heavy decrease of enlistments in the counties of Lanark and Renfrew during the past week was expressed to-day by Lieut. Purvis, district recruiting officer.
