The hon. member has spoken for forty minutes.

I understand that the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) does not wish to speak at this time. I am going to be as brief and as explicit as possible in what I have to say. I rise after listening to the last speaker in his references to recruiting, labour and so on, and I wonder, as I often wonder, when I hear discussions in the house, whether we expect to win the war here; for, as far as I can see, travelling across the country, this is where most of the war effort is being made. One thing that most members fail to recognize is that Canada's largest army to-day is in overalls.
Our greatest requirement is production. While what I have to say may not come directly within the province of the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe), his department is eventually affected. I wish to call attention to something that I had the privilege of seeing yesterday for myself. From time to time hon. members rise in their places and talk about democracy and the necessity for its preservation, and our democratic way of life, and fine phrases like that, but as far as that army in overalls is concerned anything but democracy is being practised. It is no mystery to me why we are not getting recruits voluntarily. In order to get men to fight they must be assured that they have something to fight for, and for hon. members to rise in their places and use all these fine phrases about democracy does not make it a reality, because democracy is something that is supposed to work in the lives of the people. I draw this to the minister's attention, that there is now developing in the Kirkland Lake area a situation which, if allowed to continue, will have serious repercussions not only in that area but perhaps all across Canada, and will eventually ramify into the Department of Munitions and Supply, because the same situation is developing at the Ford Motor company in Windsor where the machines are made that are so necessary to our war effort.
I remember the efforts of the workers at Kirkland Lake to accept the principles laid down by the federal government, the right to organize and bargain collectively with their employers. These men have been patient and long-suffering; they have gone along for the past fifteen or sixteen months through all the legal processes provided by the govern-
The War-Mr. Gillis

ment with respect to exercising that democracy about which we talk so much. A commission made inquiry into the situation in that district and recommended a company union. The men still carried on negotiations with the government through the Department of Labour and were successful in having another conciliation board appointed. This board unanimously recommended recognition of the union in that district. The operators refused to obey that mandate of the conciliation board. The operators refused to obey the laws of the country, and their only excuse for refusing to accept the decision of the conciliation board was that they would not do business with the C.I.O. I know something about the C.I.O. and I say that the C.I.O. does not exist in Canada at the present time. To begin with, the C.I.O. is not a trade union, it is a trade union centre. The C.I.O. does not sign collective agreements, does not negotiate wage agreements. The C.I.O. is a legislative centre for the unions in the United States; when the Canadian Congress of Labour was set up in Canada it replaced the C.I.O. in Canada, and the Canadian Congress of Labour is now the legislative centre for the industrial unions in Canada. Therefore the mine operators are very badly confused or misinformed or else are deliberately ducking the issue when they give as a reason for not accepting the mandate of this board that they will not do business with the C.I.O. They will not have to do business with the C.I.O. but will do business with their own workmen in that section once the organization is set up.
Speaking again of democracy, I consider the franchise to be the very basis of democracy. But the machinery provided by the Department of Labour for taking that vote in Kirkland Lake was a disgrace. Whoever was responsible for it made a complete mess. I was there on Sunday, attended three meetings in the afternoon, and I say that there is as well developed and as well led a trades union movement in that section as in any other part of Canada, sensible men who know where they are going and who are patient and long-suffering. Some eight or ten men from the Department of Labour went in there and conducted that vote. The men were given no opportunity to see the form of ballot that was to be used; they were given no list of those eligible to vote. Let me read the ballot; if this is not a deliberate attempt to take the franchise from the men on that question, then

I am no judge of ballots. It starts off with some straight propaganda for company unionism. It reads:
Your employer agrees to negotiate with a committee elected by the employees of the company but not with local 240 of the Mine, Mill and Smelter Workers' Union.
Are you in favour of a strike unless the company is prepared to negotiate with local 240?
Yes	
No	
That ballot is handed to these men with no opportunity given to understand it; it is a deliberate attempt to propagandize against the legitimate rights of the men in that section.
This is what I am concerned about; the main concern of any responsible executive of a trade union is to avoid trouble or head it off. Hon. members know that since I have been in this house I have continuously given warning against what would happen. For five and a half months last summer we went through a mess in Nova Scotia that would not have arisen had attention been paid to some of the things I said here. Now I see developing a similar situation in Kirkland Lake. According to the figures I see in the press the men voted in favour of a strike. Some 4,500 men are affected; an entire community is affected, and if that strike develops it is a shame and a crime on the part of those responsible for handling the situation. The men could legally have gone on strike this morning, but they postponed it until Thursday in order to give the Minister of Labour (Mr. McLarty) an opportunity for further negotiation to make the mine operators see what is fair and just.
A strike is an easy thing to call, but a hard thing to settle. The workers there have canvassed all their legal rights; if a strike takes place it is going to affect the entire labour movement in Canada, because there has been so much injustice and disregard of regular procedure in that area that the entire labour movement in Canada will take it up, and perhaps we shall have trouble from coast to coast, while all that is necessary to head it off is that someone with authority, realizing what should be done, shall settle the matter on the basis of that vote.
I bring this situation to the attention of the committee now because I know that if this continues until Thursday morning without something being done to assure the men there that their democratic rights are going to be protected, there will be trouble and that

The War-Oil and Gasoline
trouble may spread all across Canada. The people in Windsor sent a telegram which was read here the other day and we have had several letters, making the same objection to the same form of ballot. Instead of the matter being decided on the majority basis, the same basis as that on which hon. menjbers are elected to this house, the eligible vote at the mine is taken and every vote not cast is counted as a vote against the union. Yet even on that basis the union won with quite a large percentage.
In rising it was not my intention to waste time or to make a long speech. I simply wished to direct the attention of the committee and of the Minister of Munitions and Supply -because he is going to be affected sooner or later if this is allowed to continue-to the situation that exists. Instead of criticism I am presenting an appeal to those in authority to stop this, to do something about it before it goes too far.

There was a sharp reduction, as a result of the rationing. I think the August figure came very close to the figure for August last year, while the September and October figures were arbitrarily set at 20 per cent below the corresponding figures for September and October of last year.

When rationing went into effect this autumn I believe there was an increase of one cent a gallon in the retail price of gasoline. What was the reason for that increase in price? Did the companies provide the department with information indicating that an increase was necessary; and, if that information has been supplied, will the minister give it to the committee?

The increase in the price of gasoline came after some months of control, as a result of the steady increase in the price of crude. I mentioned on Friday that during the same period the price of gasoline at the gulf, which of course is where all our gasoline originates, and where transportation charges do not have to be considered, had risen two cents, while the price of gasoline in New York, where the transportation charges are much lower than to Canadian points, had risen by from 2-4 to 2-6 cents. The increase of one cent in August was looked into very carefully. All the savings that had been made possible by the oil companies through the regulations of the controller, such as cutting out the use of credit cards and similar savings, were assessed, and the companies were given considerably less than they asked. Subsequently they took their case to the war-time prices and trade board, and the situation was carefully reviewed by that board which at that time was responsible for all prices. A further increase of one cent in the price of gasoline was granted in certain areas, I think in the maritime provinces, Quebec and eastern Ontario. It was not granted in western Ontario, the prairies or British Columbia.

I should like to ask whether we shall be given a statement on what is being done in the way of reclaiming lubricating oil. I understand a process has
The War-Oil and Gasoline

been perfected by which they can take lubricating oil that has been used in aeroplane engines for a certain number of hours and, by heating it and putting it through pressure, can filter and reclaim that oil to a very high standard, at very little cost.

I think every militia camp has an oil reclaiming unit. It is my understanding that oil from the airports, as well as the oil used in the military vehicles, is sent to these militia centres, where it is reclaimed and used over again. Of course, my hon. friend will understand that it could not be used for aeroplane engines; it is not brought back to its original grade, though it is not a bad grade after being reclaimed. It can be put through this process once or twice with good results, and I believe pretty well every army vehicle is using reclaimed oil.
My information was , that in large areas of the west this was being done by private firms, that the militia units were not doing it.

I know there is one of these units at Camp Borden, because I have seen it, and I think we have purchased reclaiming outfits for all the military camps. I doubt very much if oil from either military aeroplanes or military vehicles is being refined by private firms; I should be surprised if that were the situation. I do not see how they could acquire the oil to refine it.

I wonder whether the minister or the oil controller has considered giving the farmers the right to purchase gasoline in barrels for their cars. As a rule farmers do not live within a few blocks of a service station. In many instances they are twenty, thirty or even more miles from a filling station, and in order to. buy what gasoline they can afford they are compelled to use one, two, three or perhaps more gallons of gasoline to make the trip. In my particular area the price of ethyl gasoline by the barrel is 34 cents a gallon. At the pump the same gasoline costs 39 cents a gallon, or almost the price of a bushel of wheat. I wonder whether some step could not be taken to give the farmer a small break by allowing him to buy gasoline both for automobile and truck use by the barrel, instead of compelling him to go to the pump and needlessly waste gasoline.
I think farmers have been given certain concessions that have not been extended to owners of ordinary pleasure cars. I believe a farmer is allowed to purchase gasoline in cans, is he not?
No, not for a car.

Perhaps he can purchase it in cans for his farm machines, but not for his car. I believe all this will be corrected as soon as it is possible to put in the coupon books. Then the farmer will have a coupon book which he can use at all times, and the present restrictions, which were designed to cut down the use of gasoline, of course will not apply. I dare say that at that time some arrangement can be made such as my hon. friend suggests. The ethyl gasoline to which he referred would be used for pleasure driving.

It is also used in a number of new trucks now being produced, because it gives better performance. If we were allowed to purchase in barrel quantities we would save five cents a gallon. We now pay $17.55 per 45-gallon barrel for ethyl gasoline, when purchasing locally. That is a condition which should be corrected.

The hon. member's observations illustrate the difficulty of having uniform regulations in Canada. This is a most difficult country in which to ration or control gasoline, because different areas present different conditions. I am sure, however, that the oil controller is constantly obtaining new information and solving new difficulties. The reason why we did not ration gasoline months ago is that we had to acquire a great deal of information respecting the requirements in different areas across the country. I am hopeful that when a complete rationing system comes out, it will be possible to take into account all conditions, including the ones mentioned by the hon. member.

I believe what has been said exemplifies the lack of foresight the government has shown in respect of its handling of oil. The hon. member for Davenport pointed out the necessity for the government immediately considering the possibility of utilizing the Alberta tar sands. I recall speaking particularly about the Alberta tar sands immediately after the outbreak of the war. On that occasion I pointed out that a German syndicate had offered to install a pipeline. On that occasion the Minister of Munitions and Supply answered me.
It is now evident that there is a shortage of gasoline. While in my opinion the time is long past when this matter should have been looked after. I would urge that it be done now. The government should do everything possible to increase production. It goes without question that there is a tremendous supply of oil products in the tar sands of Athabaska.

The War-Oil and Gasoline
Some money may be required to develop production. If, however, we want gasoline, then why do we not go out and get it?
It is now said that gasoline is to be rationed. I am completely mystified, because when price control was discussed some time ago the government told us that rationing could not be carried out. Yet it is now undertaking to do so. The only difficulty is that it is about two years too late in beginning. A year ago in the house I pointed out that if there was a scarcity of any commodity it would not be proper to allow the price to increase, as has been done with respect to gasoline. The proper procedure was to enforce rationing. If we are short of gasoline, let us not just fool round with the idea of rationing; let us have a strict rationing system. If we are really in need of gasoline, every pleasure car in the country should be put off the road.
At the same time I believe the present system of gasoline control is wrong, and the government is losing the confidence of the people, not only through the operation of the control now in effect, but because it is not making every endeavour to increase production. The minister has said that he placed production figures on Hansard. I looked for them this morning, but did not succeed in finding them.
I have in mind particularly the Turner valley, and the tar sands in the north. I believe that in those fields the government has done nothing more than a small amount of surveying of possibilities. I am concerned chiefly with the actual increase in oil production. I am convinced that in the last six months or the last year oil production in Canada has not been increased to any appreciable degree, certainly not to the amount it should have reached, if we really wanted to obtain gasoline.
The statement published by the Joy Oil company is astonishing. I do not believe the minister has answered it fully. One paragraph reads:
During September, 1941, we were promised tankers by the United States tanker pool, providing we secured the recommendation of Canadian oil controller, G. R. Cottrelle. Despite our repeated efforts, Cottrelle refused all our requests, and we were advised to buy our gasoline from the big Canadian oil companies.
That is a serious charge. They were short of gasoline-and I have no doubt the Minister of Munitions and Supply is right when he says there is a shortage. If we are short of gasoline, then why force this large oil company to buy from Canadian companies, when it could buy from the United States? It must be remembered, too, that this company is underselling other Canadian companies. If
I am to be robbed, I do not care if it is done by a Canadian or an American. My only concern is that I am being robbed. Surely the Imperial Oil company could sell gasoline just as cheaply as the Joy Oil company? If I am correctly informed, the Imperial Oil company is only a subsidiary of the Standard Oil company of the United States.
I can see where oil companies might gain great advantage by rationing present supplies, even to the extent of eliminating civilian consumption. I believe it would be more to their advantage to have such rationing than to have an increase in production which would take care of both civilian and war-time needs. After the war, in the event of increased production we would have an abundant supply of gasoline, and prices would naturally decrease. The oil companies which have practically a monopoly of oil production in Canada would have a tendency to keep the price up, and to cut down the supply.
I believe the government is negligent almost to the point of-yes, someone has whispered "sabotage"-when it neglects its present opportunity to increase our oil production to the maximum. The minister may say, as he did once before, that the government is not going to put money into oil production. If he does reply in that way, then I say to him, as I did before, that it is the government's business to get the gasoline. I do not care how they get it, but certainly it is their business to get it. With our potentialities there is no reason for a shortage of gasoline. The tar sands in northern Alberta are estimated to be the largest potential oil fields in the world. Not one solitary thing is being done so far as actual production is concerned. Some surveys may have been made-but that is not production.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, I had not intended to say anything to the committee, but I received a letter this morning from the secretary of the Thunder Bay Milk Producers' association. This letter draws a picture of what the farmers of that district have been going through. Their second crop of hay was lost; their wheat, oats and barley were rotting in the stook, and they have not been able to harvest their potatoes on account of wet weather. The story is told of one man with sixteen acres of
The War-Mr. Mclvor

potatoes who had to go out in top-boots and dig enough for his own use; he lost his crop. The milk producers of the district want an increase of twenty-five cents per hundredweight for milk and an increase of five cents a pound for butterfat, for cream used in the fluid trade. This application, of course, has to go before the milk control board at Toronto, and the board's decision will have to be approved by the war-time prices and trade board. The milk producers certainly are deserving of consideration. I hope also that when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) is considering the bonus question he will not forget the farmers in the Thunder bay district who have lost everything.
I hope, too, that the dependents of soldiers will receive first consideration when the bonus question is considered. The young man who has volunteered for service overseas and left his wife and children behind in Canada has certainly a better right to a bonus than the man who takes his place in civil life. Old age pensions should also be bonused.
I am sure, too, that this house will be grateful to the Minister of Finance for not adding a bonus to the salaries of the members of parliament. If such a bonus were suggested, I believe there would be a revolution in this house.
I should like to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) who was a storm centre last year because he advocated growing less wheat and more feed. The farmers of Ontario must be wishing that he had got better support then, because they are very glad now to get feed from the west.
I also want to congratulate the government upon what it has done under the war-time housing scheme at the head of the lakes. We needed houses very badly at the head of the lakes, and the government came to our assistance. A local committee was formed, consisting of A. F. Hawkens, superintendent of the Canadian Pacific Railway; C. E. Chappie, of Chappie's Limited; E. J. Saulsby, manager of Canadian Car, and P. E. Doncaster, district engineer of the public works department. That committee got to work, and the result was that forty four-roomed dwellings were constructed renting at from $22 to $25; ten six-roomed dwellings renting at $30; and two staff houses for male workers, each housing eighty-eight men, or one hundred and seventy-six altogether. In those houses the rent for a single room is $4 a week, and for a double room, $3.25 for each occupant. The people who have been able to get into these houses have expressed their delight at these

comfortable homes. I believe that thirty-six other houses are now under construction under this scheme.
I was pleased to hear the Minister of Labour (Mr. McLarty) the other day state that in future trades unionism must be interwoven with industry. I heard the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) speak to-day of how he rose from the ranks of labour, and he will take second place to nobody except perhaps myself in understanding labour men from the ground up. The government that gives the right to the worker to organize and to join any union of his choice, and ensures that it is not made a criminal offence for a man to belong to a union, is going to stand behind labour through thick and thin, and there are many of us in all groups in this house who will stand behind the government if they will carry out that policy, and who will criticize them if they do not. When I was belabouring the C.I.O., my brother-in-law, who is a doctor of sociology in the university of Michigan, said to me, "You are criticizing an organization about which you know very little," I said, "I know some bad things about it, and the way to help is to advertise the bad in it." He said that those who were responsible for the C.I.O. were the craft unions because they did not organize completely and include everybody in the industry. I found it to be true in the case of the Great Lakes Pulp and Paper company at Fort William, that they included everybody in their union without the C.I.O. The man who works with a shovel and does ordinary labouring work has just as much right to protection as any other man. I know there are things in the C.I.O. that are not very good. We shall have to watch the organization closely. Nevertheless any man who toils has to fight for his own good.
Turning to another matter, I would suggest to the government that we arrange for an exchange of ministers with Russia, for two reasons: First, the change that Russia has undergone and the change in our own attitude towards Russia. I can well remember the time when Russia wanted total disarmament by all countries, but got very little support. That was the day when the League of Nations began to slip a bit. Second, our own attitude to Russia changed completely when they announced freedom of religion and that they would allow a man to worship God as he pleases. That is what we appreciate in this country. Our attitude toward Russia also changed when, instead of being a potential enemy, she became an ally. Therefore I think it would be a wise move on the part of the government to arrange for an exchange of ministers with Russia.

The War-Mr. Howe
I am not going to say much about what is going to happen after the war, but it is most hopeful when minister after minister, led by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) himself, says that after this war things are not going to be as they were after the last war. I can well remember when I struggled hard going about in my Ford car to try to find a returned man work at twenty-five cents an hour and could not find it. I do not think that day will ever come again. I hope we have learned a great deal since then, and when minister after minister rises in his place and says that we shall have a new social order after this war, a Christian social order, it gives us a good deal of hope. There are two things that I should like to see in this new Christian social order when it comes. I should like the Sabbath day to be a day of rest when a man can go to worship where he pleases. The other thing is this. We have heard a great deal about the control of gasoline in one way and another, but I have not heard a word said about the control of another liquid that is used by far more people than use gasoline. That is a matter which should be given consideration by the government.

I should like to ask the Minister of Munitions and Supply whether any plans have been made for the operation of the merchant ships and for their manning. The minister announced in the house the other day that we would have approximately one hundred merchant ships in operation by the end of next year, and I believe there are to be fifty more in the following year. Large crews will be required to operate these vessels. I am not aware that any men are now being trained for that purpose, and I would ask the minister to explain to the committee just what the situation is at the present time with regard to crews.

The Department of Transport has taken in hand the task of training crews for merchant ships. Manning pools have been established at Halifax and Montreal and are now in operation. Training schools are also being built in connection with these manning pools. It is the intention to pursue an intensive programme of enlisting and training candidates for the merchant marine.
Will there not be schools on both coasts?

I assume that there will also be a school on the west coast. I am not sure what the plans are for that. This is a new activity; it is just getting nicely under way. But I have no doubt that there will be training schools on the west coast as well. Of course, the advantage of working in connection
with manning pools is that every man graduating from a school can be assured of being placed.
How are they to be operated? By War-time Merchant Shipping, Limited, or by the government, or by private companies? That is, once the ships are actually carrying cargo?

There again, I assume that the ships being built for Canada will be operated by the Canadian government merchant marine which was organized for that purpose in the last war and is now operating ships that have been seized as prizes of war in Canadian waters. I should imagine that would be the method of operation. But of course, the recruiting and training of merchant seamen constitute an operation which is carried on in connection with all British ships. Some of our ships are being built for Great Britain, on order from Great Britain, and some are being built on Canadian orders.
Would it be against the public interest to disclose how many are for British order, and how many for Canadian?
I believe that either twenty-six or twenty-eight ships are on British order, and the balance are Canadian.

Apparently there is a shortage of steel. I see by a press report in the Vancouver Sun on November 3, that Mr. MacMillan, head of War-time Merchant Shipping, Limited, is quoted as saying:
Shortage of steel for the ships has been and still is a serious problem. It has slowed up the programme considerably in all parts. There is not enough steel produced in Canada for all war purposes and the United States defence programme, now gathering real momentum, has cut down the amount that can be got from there.
Mr. MacMillan said that experts have assured him that there will be plenty of steel by late next spring. He hopes they are right.
Could the minister tell us whether or not that report is correct?

I would say that the shortage of steel is not as severe as is indicated in the newspaper extract which my hon. friend has just read. Steel, of course, is short in Canada. We have doubled the production of steel in Canada since the war began, but we have always imported steel from the United States, and we still do, and in about the same relative proportion to our own production as formerly. Usually, I believe, steel for about one-third of our Canadian production is imported from the United States. One difficulty was that we started a shipbuilding programme at several yards at exactly the same time; each yard required the same type of steel at the same time; and we had a
The War-Mr. Howe

limited capacity for the individual ships. Another difficulty is that certain structural shapes which go into the ships have to be imported; they are heavier than any mill in Canada can roll. Just at the time we required them, the United States changed its system of priorities, and it has taken some time to get the system established. But the steel position in November is going to be very much better than in October, and I should say that by the end of the year no shipyard- at least, on present indications-will be short of steel. We have had, however, to curtail the amount of steel moving into domestic uses. We are letting the very minimum quantity of steel go into non-war uses at the moment. Practically every ton of billets that is being manufactured in Canada is being rolled into plate for ships or armour-plate or gun-barrel forgings or some use of that kind.

Have we not now reached a time when wooden ships could be used to advantage? If steel is scarce, would it not be wise for War-time Merchant Shipping, Limited, to undertake also the building of wooden cargo vessels? I understand that this can be done, that there are men available who have had training in building wooden ships. Would it not be well for Canada now to branch out into the building of wooden vessels as well as steel ones?

The question of whether or not wooden ships should be built received very careful consideration. Speaking personally, I became less and less enthusiastic as I studied the situation. The plain fact of the matter is that the cost per ton of the wooden ship is at least as great as and perhaps somewhat greater than the cost per ton of the steel ship. Operating costs are considerably higher for wooden ships than for steel ships. It must be quite obvious, I think, to all hon. members, that a timber ship would have no post-war value, and that the same man-hours put into a steel ship would produce much more value, even for war time, than the same man-hours put into a timber ship.
It may be said that a different class of labour is used in the construction of a timber ship. That is true to only a limited extent. The hulls of ships are, of course, a great deal less than half the cost of the ship; they are, perhaps, no more than one-third of the cost; and it is only the steel hull as against the wooden hull that we are discussing. For the interior fittings we draw on the same manufacturing resources for the steel ship as for the wooden ship.
As far as the Department of Munitions and Supply is concerned, and viewing the matter i*olely from that point of view, we of course

build on order from someone. We usually have a customer for the gun or tank or ship or whatever we build, before we build it. We have no appropriations of our own excepting for ordinary running expenses. If the Department of National Defence for Naval Services want a corvette, they come to us with a certificate of encumbrance, plus the order for the corvette, turn over the money to us, and we build the corvette and deliver it to them. That applies to everything which we build. While we have had no customer for a wooden ship, we have had many people come forward quite willing to build those ships; we have had nobody come forward to say that they want them.
Who would order the ships? The navy, or the Department of Transport?
It might be the merchant marine, or it might be the Canadian shipping board.
Who is the Canadian shipping board?
The Canadian shipping board is a board that operates under the Department of Trade and Commerce.
Under the instructions of the government?
Yes.

Well, then, we can tell them to buy them. Am I to understand- if I may ask a question in connection with this matter of the wooden ships-that the urgency of the situation is surmounted by the dollars and cents point of view? Is that correct?
No, I would not say that.
I understood the minister just now to say that.

We have tried in our war manufacturing to turn out a good article, and I think we have succeeded very well. If we build a ship, we build a ship which is a good ship compared with any on the ocean. If we build a tank, it is a good tank; if we build a gun, it is a good gun, equal to any. I think that when you turn out a wooden ship in this day and generation, you are turning out a second-class article, and one which hardly justifies the man-hours and the material which you put into it.

Do I understand that the minister's point is that the building of wooden ships would interfere with the construction of steel ships?

The War-Mr. Howe
Yes. Of course the engines for wooden ships come from the same factories which build engines for the steel ships.

I have in mind that it should be possible to increase the number of ships which Canada can build, by building these wooden ships in addition to the steel ships. That is the argument, I believe, which is being advanced.

Of course you can build wooden hulls without competing materially with the steel hulls, although there is a good deal of steel even in a wooden hull. When you come to all the fittings of the ship you are stepping into the same factories that are building interior fittings for the steel ships, and with a little greater effort you could get a steel hull as well as you could a timber one.

Where are you
getting the steel?
We are getting it.

I understood the minister to say he could not get sufficient
steel.
We are doing all right so far.
Am I to understand the minister to say that we are building a sufficient number of ships to meet the emergency?
We look upon Britain as a great shipbuilding country and it has been building ships for a great many years. It is still building ships; every yard is full
England is still being bombed, too.

In the next year, 1942, we expect that Canada will turn out about the same tonnage of merchant ships as Britain will, which I think, for a country that was building no ships prior to the war, will not be a bad effort. In addition, we shall have a large naval programme which will also be turning out ships in our yards. There is, however, a limit to the extent of our effort in any direction, and I doubt whether we can go into a big programme of building timber ships without crippling our efforts in the direction of steel building.

I would urge upon the minister that the question be considered very carefully. In the war effort, we have been inclined to think we could not do certain things and then the next week, by the pressure of events, we have found that we can do them. I fancy that the building of wooden ships will sooner or later exemplify that truth. I urge that he have his department or 14873-267
whoever is responsible for the decision review the whole position again. It may be that we are missing something that would be of great help in the war effort.
I shall be glad to do so.
Wooden ships at present are being built at Shelburne and Yarmouth, N.S. I understand that there are three under way. They are, I believe, going into the merchant marine service.

Those are Fairmile ships. They are of the mine-sweeper type and are being built for our own navy and the British navy. That is a highly specialized timber ship built of mahogany and to naval specifications. It is a naval vessel.

There is very little steel in these ships, and their construction certainly gives work to those skilled in this art in that part of Canada. It seems to me that if there is a shortage of that class of craft there is an abundance of room for immediate expansion of work. I have seen the work going on. At the very most there were only ten men working on one hull and probably six or eight on another, and the mill which was operating the band-saws to turn out cribwork and what-not did not have a staff of sawyers of more than a dozen. I do not believe that there was more than 150 horse-power in use, and a few ox teams for hauling in the logs, at a speed of two or three miles an hour, did not strike me as adequate. I do not wish to criticize, but I would point out that the lumber is there, and the people who have lived in that area on the Atlantic coast for many generations are accustomed to that class of work. I repeat, therefore, that there is certainly an abundance of room for a little more energy being put into that work. If, as the minister says, these particular wooden ships are efficient for a certain class of work, I should be glad if he would answer my question. I should like to have him outline the policy to show what is being done, not only in these two small yards but in many others in Nova Scotia.
I think my hon. friend is getting rather mixed up between two programmes.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, during the discussion on wooden ships I recited a case that is actually being discussed under this item, and properly so, and the minister rises in his place and says that the hon. member is getting mixed up. If he sees fit I would ask him to withdraw that remark. I think he is out of order in saying that I am mixed up.

The War-Mr. Nicholson

I withdraw. I will put it in another way. The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) was speaking, I believe, about quite another programme of ships than that to which my hon. friend was referring. My hon. friend was discussing the small boat programme which is being carried out in fifty-four yards from one end of Canada to the other. We have built nearly 800 ships in these shipyards and we are still building them. Wooden ships are being built all along the Atlantic coast and on the great lakes as well as on the Pacific coast, but these are small-boat programmes and the boats are being built in yards suitable to that type. The hon. member for Vancouver South was referring to cargo boats which would have to be built in yards of the type suitable for steel ship construction, or new yards would have to be established of that general nature for the building of merchant ships. The programme to which the hon. member for Vancouver South was referring was not the same as the programme which my hon. friend was discussing.

I wish to direct a few questions to the Minister of Munitions and Supply, but before doing so, I should like to make one or two remarks with regard to war-time housing. A dispatch from the minister's office points out that on October 27 there were twenty-seven cities and towns from coast to coast where war-time housing had been under way. According to this information we have appropriated $15,-
750,000	to complete projects that were authorized up to that date. We have provided for 4,427 houses, thirty-five staff houses and four dining halls. The sum of money mentioned might appear to be a large commitment, but if one thinks of it in terms of the entire appropriations for the Department of Munitions and Supply, it will seem small. According to the information the minister gave the other day, he has authorized to date contracts totalling $2,600,000,000. It is difficult for most of us to think in terms of such vast sums. I was examining the public accounts over the week-end, and I noticed that our entire war expenditures-demobilization expenditures included-during and since the last war totalled $1,695,000,000. In other words, this one department has awarded contracts for nearly $1,000,000,000 in excess of our entire war bill and costs since the last great war. If we add all our dominion government expenditures since 1868 chargeable to consolidated revenue fund, to capital, for railway subsidies, for war and demobilization, and for other charges until 1935, as reported on IMr. J. H. Harris.]
page 62 of the public accounts for the year ended March 31, 1941, we find a total of some $11,704,150,309, or about five times the amount of the expenditures in this one department.
When hon. members consider the tremendous development all across Canada in order to carry out the programme outlined by the minister, they will see how closely the supply of housing for the men working in the various industries is tied up with our whole industrial output. During the last great war it was not until 1918 that the matter of supplying housing was recognized as a national war emergency. But the situation during the last war was very different from what we find to-day. At the commencement of the last war we had a surplus of from 7 to 15 per cent of vacant houses in Canada. At the commencement of the present war it was less than one per cent. In addition to this, during the ten years preceding the outbreak of the war little was done in Canada to replace obsolete houses that were wearing out. It is estimated that we have about 2,500,000 housing units in Canada, and assuming that the life of the average house is fifty years we should be building 50,000 houses each year to provide for normal replacement, without making any provision for the new houses required as a result of shifts in population and the establishment of new families. But instead of building 50,000 houses a year, according to the information in Maclean's building reports we built in 1940, 20,933 houses; in 1939, 21,946; in 1938, 18,565; in 1937, 18,284, and for the years 1932 to 1936, an average of less than
12,000	a year. Thus it can be readily understood that we entered this war with a serious shortage of housing.
In peace time, with a large number of people unemployed, it is possible for two or three families to be housed together in one building; but when the men go back to work, start receiving wages, coming home from work at all hours of the day or night, it is only natural that families desire to have individual houses. It is not conducive to efficiency to have several families living in one house and the sleep of the workers disturbed by men coming and going. Therefore we find large shifts in our population, large military and naval encampments about the country where people have brought their families and are finding great difficulty in securing accommodation.
I am very glad that early in the war the government recognized that this was becoming a national problem and appropriated a sum of money. I am not, however, satisfied with the administration of war-time housing as I see it. I was asked by our caucus to

The War-Mr. Nicholson
make a special study of this problem, and I have received letters from people all across the dominion. I explained to the minister last session that in taking up this problem I had no desire to discover any scandal; that is the last thing I would wish. The minister was very kind in his attitude. There should, however, be someone in Ottawa in a position to discuss with any hon. member the activities of war-time housing, who could satisfy us that the taxpayers of Canada are receiving good value for the money spent. I felt that the set-up we had for national housing should have been used for the supervising and organizing of the war-time activities.
In 1935 the Dominion Housing Act was passed; since 1938 we have had the National Housing Act, and I am sure hon. members are pleased with the progress made by this fairly new branch of government administration. We have spent a large sum of money in making it possible for quite a large proportion of the Canadian people to have much better housing than they could have without this scheme, and this has been done at a very low monetary outlay. We had men in this administration who were familiar with housing programmes in the United States, in Europe and in all countries where really progressive work has been done in providing housing for the people. But instead of using the government administration we brought in Mr. Pigott, one of the dollar-a-year men. I say nothing against Mr. Pigott; he has to his credit some of Canada's very finest buildings, but being able to place one's services at the disposal of the country for a dollar a year does not necessarily qualify one to do a job such as that of president of War-time Housing Limited. Mr. Goggin, the general manager, must also be a very good man because we are paying him a very good salary, $10,000 a year, enough to secure the services of the best men in the housing field. I feel, however, that we are not using the personnel or the research work which has been available under our national housing administration.
I have not been able to secure the information that I think I am entitled to as a member of parliament. I wrote to War-time Housing Limited early in the summer saying that since I had been assigned to this work I should like to be supplied with as full information as possible regarding the activities of war-time housing all across the country. On August 7 I had a reply from the general manager giving the names of places where war-time housing was active and the number of houses in each place. It did not give any information regarding the type of buildings, terms of contracts, rentals charged, or information from which to judge
whether they were really dealing with the problem as it should be dealt with. While I have not had a great many complaints, the information I have is that there is much to be desired in connection with the operation of war-time housing. A letter from St. Catharines makes complaints regarding an unusual clause in the lease. They rent only on a month-to-month basis; a tenant must give one month's notice when leaving, but it is stipulated that a tenant may be asked to leave on only three days' notice. The argument advanced is that war-time housing want to prevent the area becoming run down or houses being used for bootlegging or prostitution. No doubt their objective is worthy, but it seems to me that asking people to vacate on three days' notice is unreasonable. The rents charged are not especially low, $22 to $30, similar to the rents mentioned in Fort William. I believe this parliament is entitled to more information regarding the activities of war-time housing.
If the minister had time at his disposal to supervise work on housing, no doubt it would be very well done, but with $2,600,000,000 being spent by the Department of Munitions and Supply, it is almost impossible for him to be in close touch with all that is going on in the hundred and one different branches under his supervision. I believe there should be in his department in Ottawa some civil servant who is familiar with everything that is being done by war-time housing. I think in the Department of Finance there should be some official with complete information as to the types of construction, the nature of contracts and so on, who would be in a position to assure members of parliament that the people of Canada are getting good value for the money that is being spent.
May I conclude with five or six questions which I should like the minister to answer if he can do so. First, would the minister tell the committee why the staff of the national housing administration could not have been extended and used to carry out whatever wartime housing building programmes were necessary. Second, what check is there by the Department of Finance and/or the Department of Munitions and Supply on the types of construction and materials of war-time housing projects? Third, what has been the cost per unit for the housing units completed in any of the centres where houses have been completed? Fourth, what is the largest number of pre-fabricated houses constructed by any one firm? Fifth, what are the estimated expenditures in connection with the entire building programme as at present contemplated by War-time Housing Limited? Sixth, what policy has been followed in connection
The War-Housing

with the purchase of materials in general, and heating units in particular, by War-time Housing Limited for the 4,400 houses which have been built? I am not sure that the minister can answer .these questions at the moment, but I would appreciate it if he could.

I think, when my hon. friend has time to investigate more closely, he will find War-time Housing Limited to be a very efficient operation indeed. About a month ago I had the pleasure of going to Hamilton to take part in the opening of a staff house. While there, I investigated a number of housing projects in that neighbourhood. One thing that struck me was the very attractive appearance of these houses. In any block of them, out of five houses not one will be exactly like any other; they are well spaced, and so on. I was particularly interested in the reaction of those who had just moved into the houses. I had a talk with one man and asked him how he liked his house. He spoke in very high praise of it and said, "I will put it this way. A few years ago I built a brick-veneer house that cost me $5,200. If I could swap even for this house I would be delighted to do so." The house to which he was referring was one of the smallest of the war-time housing units, a four-roomed house which cost about $1,800 or, with plumbing, local improvements and so on, perhaps $2,000 or $2,100. Getting that reaction, which I got almost everywhere I went, it struck me that we had built something the public were receiving favourably, and that a good job had been done.
Was that a $5,200 house which was used as a comparison?
Yes.
Compared with the smallest unit in this housing scheme?

Yes. I am simply repeating what this man told me. I am not suggesting that the trade could have been made, or anything like that, but that was what he told me.
My hon. friend referred to the huge amount my department has spent. Well, we have placed a great many contracts and spent a tremendous amount of money, and the reason why we have had no scandals and no great difficulties is that the department is very highly organized. We have chosen the best men in the industry to carry on this undertaking. We have had a very good treasury staff; and while I read in the papers that we have made mistakes, frankly I do not know what they are. Perhaps some day those who say we have made mistakes will tell us what they have been, but in the meantime it seems to me we have been getting on very well. We organized War-time Housing Limited very 
carefully. We chose Mr. Pigott to head the company because I think he is at the top of his profession in that particular type of construction. We had associated with him a Canadian architect who all his life has specialized in that type of housing, and on the board of directors we placed men who took a very great interest in that type of work.
The first question my hon. friend asks is why the national housing administration staff was not extended to handle the work. The reason, of course, is that their work is along quite a different line. The national housing staff administers the government's responsibility largely in private construction; in other words, the houses over which the national housing staff have jurisdiction are largely built by private owners, to standards and specifications fixed by the national housing administration, but the main job of the housing administration is to see that the loan guaranteed by the government on those houses is properly secured. War-time housing had a very difficult task. It had to go into heavily congested industrial areas and build houses to take care of a temporary situation. It was concerned with a type of house that need not be a permanent affair, in case there should be another shift of population away from that area.

I notice that in the September 11 issue of The Lachute Watchman it is stated that the national housing administration supplied the plans and specifications for the very large project at Sorel, Quebec. It seems to me they have already done a good deal of work in preparing plans and specifications for the very sort of work that War-time Housing Limited has done.

I can explain why that is so. The Sorel gun plant and shipbuilding plant, as my hon. friend knows, were privately owned at the beginning of the war. The government has made some investment in the gun plant, in its programme of expansion, and the houses are more or less a joint operation, partly privately owned and partly financed by the government. The housing project there was undertaken before War-time Housing Limited was organized, and at my suggestion the national housing administration did take charge of that programme for both private and government interests. They designed and supervised the construction of the houses at Sorel, but so far as I know that is the only case where the national housing administration has actually designed and supervised the construction of houses as a complete job.

The War-Housing
Why could they not have extended their operations all across Canada?

They could, but we decided to do it in another way, and I think we were wise. We organized a staff which I do not think could have been organized under the national housing plan. In any event, the national housing administration has a very large programme of its own. The houses that are to be built by War-time Housing Limited are very few in number compared with the houses being built under the national housing plan, even at the present time.
Then my hon. friend asks what check there is by the Department of Finance and/or the Department of Munitions and Supply on the types of construction and materials in war-time housing projects. There is the very closest check. Officers of the Department of Finance check every item that goes into any war-time housing project. The treasurer of War-time Housing Limited is an officer of the Department of Finance. The auditor is the auditor general of Canada, and every dollar spent by war-time housing is handled by the Department of Finance. The buying for War-time Housing Limited is supervised by the purchasing branch of the Department of Munitions and Supply, which is aware of the price paid for everything that is bought and which makes sure that every discount to which the government is entitled is secured, and that the lowest price obtainable by the government is obtained by War-time Housing Limited.
Are tenders asked for?
Yes, they are always asked for.
Are the municipalities protected in so far as taxes for school purposes are concerned?

Yes. I will explain that.
The next question is: What has been the cost per unit for the housing units completed in any of the centres where houses have been completed? From one end of Canada to the other, I would say that the houses themselves, including plumbing and heating, cost between $1,800 and $2,100 per unit.
Without the land?

Yes, and without furniture. That includes only the house itself, which may be built on posts. In many instances we take an undeveloped lot and put in sewage, and all the improvements that go with the land. In some instances that brings up the cost to another thousand dollars. I
should be very glad to analyse the various projects, and if my hon. friend would put a question on the order paper I will see that a return is made.
The next question is: What is the largest number of prefabricated houses constructed by any one firm? I believe the largest number is the contract with the Brookfield Construction company at Halifax. That has been a continuing contract, and runs into about two thouand houses.
All in Halifax?

I think there are 2,800 houses there altogether.
The next question is: What are the estimated expenditures in connection with the entire building programme as at present contemplated by War-time Housing Limited? The total amount authorized to date is between $15,000,000 and $16,000,000.

I notice there have not been any projects undertaken in any of the prairie provinces. We have an acute shortage in many of our cities, and I wonder whether the plan as at present contemplated does not envisage an extension in many centres where the shortage is acute.
These houses are entirely for the purpose of housing munitions workers.
W'hat about Winnipeg?

Winnipeg was a city where there were many vacant houses. I suppose before the war there was no city which had as large a number of vacant houses as had Winnipeg. I have heard of no shortage there, but if a shortage occurs we will meet it. We have been building only in cities where there is a shortage of houses. I believe I have answered the last question as to the policy followed in purchasing materials in general, and heating units. Those are being purchased under the supervision of the purchasing branch of the Department of Munitions and Supply.
Are prices asked for?
We buy in large units. We buy for the whole project.

I rise, not to ask a question of the minister, but rather to correct what appears to be a wrong impression in the mind of the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson), when he referred to the status of Mr. Pigott, president of War-time Housing Limited. I think the hon. member's understanding could arise only from his not knowing Mr. Pigott, or the reputation he has throughout Canada. I can say from personal

The War-Housing
knowledge that Mr. Pigott is a man of the highest integrity and ability. He has a reputation of doing his work thoroughly and well, and is to be entirely relied upon in any of his undertakings. He has had a long experience in one of the leading contracting firms in Canada, and I do not think anyone better qualified could have been appointed to the job.
The hon. member is imputing to me motives I had no intention of expressing.
I am not imputing motives at all.
The hon. member has drawn the inference that I cast some reflection upon Mr. Pigott's integrity. I did nothing of the sort.
What about school taxation?

An arrangement has been made between War-time Housing Limited and the municipalities in which it builds. The arrangement has been ratified by all the provinces in which these houses have been erected. The government pays to the municipality a flat rate per house sufficient to cover school taxes and, I believe, a small amount in addition. I am not familiar with the exact details, but I know that each province and each city in which houses have been built have approved the arrangement.

I am not interested in what each of the provinces may do, because we have had certain experiences in British Columbia. They will approve anything in connection with school costs.
I must apologize for reverting to the subject of shipping, but I did not have the privilege of being in the house when the minister was speaking in this connection. During the last twenty-four hours I have had to stay near a telephone. A certain convention is being held, and I have been holding myself in readiness to accept any nomination which might come my way.
To return to the subject of shipping, I understood the minister to say there was a shortage of oil, and he gave as a reason a shortage of tankers. In that connection I would quote from possibly the best paper in the Dominion of Canada, namely, the Vancouver Daily Province of February 22, 1941. I hope the reporters in the gallery hear what I said about that paper. Speaking in British Columbia, the minister said:
It has more ship orders than any other province. The yards are filled to capacity until the end of 1942.

Since that time many orders have been given in British Columbia. We have since launched our first steel cargo ship. And yet, according to what the minister is recorded to have said, as reported at page 4192 of Hansard, when he was speaking about oil, we still have not enough shipping. He said:
The refiners have had to contend with a very sharp rise in the price of crude oil, and they have had to contend also with greatly increased transportation costs.
I presume the minister meant that increased transportation costs had been brought about through a shortage of shipping. He has stated before that it is not practicable to build wooden ships, and that because of their longer life steel ships are more practicable. Yet we are short of oil.
I must apologize again for reverting to the subject of oil, but there may be some explanation for the question which is in my mind. I know the people in the constituency of Fraser Valley and in the city of North Vancouver want to have the answer. May I repeat what the minister said:
The refiners have had to contend with a very sharp rise in the price of crude oil, and they have had to contend also with greatly increased transportation costs.
I do not expect an answer right away, but I should like the minister to state what these increased transportation costs are. So far as I know, there is no increase in transportation costs between California and Vancouver. Much of our oil prior to the war came in, not by tanker but by tank car. I have yet to learn that there is a shortage of tank cars.
Again, as reported at page 4192 of Hansard, the minister stated, in his explanation as to the increase in price:
-that is, two cents based on the small United States gallon, which is somewhat more when translated into cost, in Canadian money, of the Canadian gallon.
All hon. members know the difference in size between United States and Canadian gallons, but we also know that every major oil company operating in Canada is controlled in the United States, and they enjoy a benefit of approximately ten cents on the dollar.
I do not expect an answer right away, but I would ask the minister to state at his convenience what the increase in cost of transportation of gasoline delivered to British Columbia amounts to. I would also ask why these oil companies, with a ten per cent exchange advantage, are entitled to an increase of one cent a gallon. Each and every major oil company operating in Canada is controlled in the United States and, as one hon. member has stated, they are actually selling oil to themselves.

The War-Oil
There may be a shortage, but with all due deference, I suggest there is no shortage in British Columbia. If there is a shortage, we are willing to submit to rationing to-morrow or any day. At present, however, I do not think there is a shortage. One oil company in California selling oil to its own subsidiary company in British Columbia receives an increase of one cent a gallon, plus the figure mentioned by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reidi) of a certain amount in lieu of credit cards. Yet they pass none of that on to the little distributor. Nobody can tell me that the big oil companies have not had a wider and more profitable market for their gas since the war. Now, instead of selling to the small distributor, they sell by the hundreds of thousands of gallons to the dominion government and the Department of Munitions and Supply. They are selling more gasoline than they ever sold before in British Columbia, and they get an increase of one cent a gallon, which is not passed on to the little distributor, but is kept by the big oil companies themselves. I do not want to be critical, but that situation does not make sense to me. Nothing has caused more dissatisfaction in British Columbia.
I accepted the explanation of the minister in connection with the Joy Oil company. I did not know there was a Joy Oil company. It certainly has not caused much joy in British Columbia. Rightly or wrongly, we in that province think the oil controller is playing into the hands of the big companies and is operating in their interests. The minister can dispel that idea in so far as my riding is concerned if he can show me that the cost of transportation from California or Texas or Oklahoma to British Columbia has increased, and if he can show me that these companies in California, Texas and Oklahoma are not selling to a subsidiary company in Canada, thereby getting the benefit of the ten per cent, and in addition one cent a gallon increase. I think I am entitled to an explanation. Personally I do not know anything about the oil business, but I do not believe there is a particle of shortage of gasoline in British Columbia, in spite of the figures that have been given by Mr. Cottrelle. With all due deference to Mr. Cottrelle I do not think he realizes the situation in western Canada or in western United States. We see in the papers to-day that the United States has lifted all gasoline restrictions on the eastern coast. Yet in spite of everything the long-suffering poor Standard Oil company has to have one cent a gallon increase, plus all the credit charges, and the only justification given is the vague statement that the increase is due to transportation costs. If the minister can explain the situation satisfactorily to me,
I may be able to explain it to my constituents, but he is going to have a hard time explaining to me that the oil companies are suffering as was intimated in that statement. Will the minister give me an explanation?
I cannot at this moment discuss transportation costs on the British Columbia coast, and my hon. friend was fair enough to say that he did not expect me to.
But the minister will in the future?

I said it was partly due to the increased cost of crude, which I know to be a fact. I do not know exactly what the increase has been in the Los Angeles area, where British Columbia oil comes from in the main, or how much tankers have gone up. My hon. friend says that in British Columbia they have been accustomed to get their gasoline in tank cars. I venture the statement that not two per cent of the gasoline used in British Columbia has come in there in tank cars in the last ten years. You would have a very sorry situation if you had to depend on any considerable movement of oil in tank cars. If my hon. friend will put a question on the order paper for exactly the information he wants, I will try to get it.
Thank you. Shall I get it this session or have to wait until January?
It depends upon how complicated the question is.

It is a simple
question.

I should like to ask a question with respect to the shipbuilding programme.
The discussion is getting mixed up with housing and oil. I would ask the minister what progress is being made in reconditioning the big steel mill at Sydney, Nova Scotia, to roll plate for shipbuilding. It is felt in our part of Canada that this work is very much behind, in preparing for this very necessary programme of shipbuilding. I should like to know when it is expected that plates will be rolled, also what outlay is being made by the department to enable these plates to be rolled, and what assured use there will be for these plates.
I should also like a statement from the minister as to the steel shipbuilding programme in Nova Scotia. We have been much disappointed that up to the present there has been only what I might call a political promise that shipbuilding will be undertaken at Pictou, Nova Scotia, while on the western coast, in

The War-Munitions and Supply
Montreal, and on the great lakes ships are actually being launched; but in Nova Scotia the steel shipbuilding programme is only being projected, though it is recognized by practically everybody that Nova Scotia should be in the very forefront and be given a preference in a programme of this kind.
I should also like a statement from the minister as to what yards are projected in Nova Scotia to carry on this shipbuilding programme?
My hon. friend speaks of a political promise of shipyards. I may say that my hon. friend himself is the one man who can never forget politics when asking any question.

That statement is not fair. The minister himself is the one minister who made a political promise with respect to war expenditures on aeroplane factories. I think he was the only minister who in a political campaign sent a telegram to be read at a political meeting, stating that if so-and-so were done, an aeroplane factory would be built at Amherst.
And was it?
It was a political promise of public money provided for war purposes by all the people of Canada, and the minister made it a political issue on the platform.
On what platform did I say anything about it?
The minister's telegram was read from the platform in Amherst in the last federal campaign.

I am not responsible for what is read on a political platform. I certainly never mentioned Amherst in any political speech that I made in any part of the country. If my hon. friend will forget politics for a moment and talk about the war, we shall get on faster.
So far as the plate mill in Sydney is concerned, it is being brought into production as rapidly as possible. I understand that the date on which it will be put into operation depends upon the delivery of some heavy motors which are being manufactured at the present time. They are somewhat behind schedule, but I hope the mill will be in operation in February or March of next year, contingent on the delivery of those motors.
We are somewhat short of plate capacity at the present time; not unduly short, because we are rolling every billet we can manufacture. Our billet capacity is increasing, and the plates from Sj'dney will be needed.
IMr. P. C. Black.]
As far as new shipyards are concerned, we have only two new ones in contemplation at the present time, one in Vancouver, which is now laying its first keel, and one at Pictou, which is suitable for the present programme of ships. I do not know what other questions there were.
I asked the minister what commitments have been made and what outlet there will be for the projected production of the rolling mill at Sydney; also, what its expected tonnage output per year will be.

I rather think the capacity of that mill when it is in operation will be about
12,000	tons a month. I judge that from what I know of the capacity of the mill. Getting back to the matter of the distribution of the billets which can be produced at the mill, I may say that every billet is being used now, and if we had the mill in operation now it would be used pretty well to capacity. I daresay that condition will continue.
There is additional blast furnace capacity, is there not?
Additional blast furnace capacity is being brought in, and there is a plant under way at the present time to increase the production of pig.
Is that being financed by the minister's department or by the government? I refer to these additions and new facilities.

Partly by the company itself and partly by the government. I believe the total expenditure under way runs to about five and a half million dollars, of which four million dollars is represented by a loan from the government.
I did not like the retort of the minister, in his political reference to myself.
Just why did the hon. member need to mention "political promises"?

My basis for that is that, while ships are being launched in other parts of Canada, it was during the political campaign in Nova Scotia during the past few weeks that the announcement was made by the minister of industry and publicity and the premier of Nova Scotia that a shipyard was to be started in Pictou. That was the first public notification we had that such a programme was to be carried out. I think it is unfortunate that it should have been announced in that way. I ask the minister to advise me or advise the committee why the announce-

The War-Munitions and Supply
ment with respect to the programme in Nova Scotia has been delayed, while ships of a similar nature are being actually launched in other parts of Canada. It is a matter of discrimination, or was so interpreted in Nova Scotia. I think it is reasonable on my part to ask the minister why the programme in Nova Scotia has been delayed. I think we should have this information.
The programme of shipbuilding was discussed in this chamber in previous sessions by hon. members from the maritimes. The contention was made, and was supported by hon. members from Toronto and other parts of Canada, that Nova Scotia and the maritime provinces have not had a fair share of the distribution of moneys for government works having to do with the war. In shipbuilding, for which above everything else they should have had the preference, they are the last place in Canada to receive recognition. Nova Scotia is the last place where a programme for building steel merchant ships has been announced. It was announced for political advantage during an election. It does not seem to me that sort of thing creates a good atmosphere wherein to carry on the war. There should be no political pressure or political advantage in order to carry out programmes of this kind. As I have said, it is not my intention to be critical of the minister, but I believe we are entitled to some explanation with respect to the shipbuilding programme in eastern Canada.

The remarks of my hon. friend illustrate exactly the point I made a few minutes ago. What he takes exception to indicates the fundamental difference between my viewpoint and his. My viewpoint about ships is that I want to get the maximum number for use during the war period. My purpose in building ships is not to enrich any one section of this country or to glorify any particular town, or city, or province. My object is to get ships where I can get them most quickly and cheaply. The reason why we built ships where we have built them is that there were organizations there which understood how to build ships, and slipways which would take ships. We filled those first. Then we looked round to see where we could increase shipbuilding capacity, and we found that the places where we could increase it reasonably were very few; in fact, there were only two. We found in Vancouver two steel companies which were in a position to combine and build slipways and launch ships, without the necessity of robbing existing shipyards of their skilled personnel.
Will the minister say which firm that is?
That is a combination of, I think it is, Vancouver Engineering works and one or two steel companies there.
It is quite a good riding, anyway.

I do not even remember the name. The other place we found was at Pictou. What we found at Pictou was not, by any means, a readymade shipyard, but a certain amount of skilled personnel was available there. I may say that we searched Nova Scotia and New Brunswick from one end to the other to try to find the nucleus of an organization which could handle a steel shipbuilding project of this magnitude. We found it at Pictou. After a good deal of discussion and negotiation, including considerations of capital assistance and additional skilled personnel which had to be furnished, the project reached the point where an announcement could be made. Now my hon. friend says it was announced during an election. I do not think he could expect us to stop the war for three or four weeks so as to get that election over.

My complaint is that the announcement was not made by the minister or by the federal government; it was made by a provincial minister while running an election in that province, and on behalf of the premier of Nova Scotia.

I do not suppose. that one could keep it very much of a secret. Negotiations were going on between this group at Pictou and war-time merchant shipping, and I assume that the premier had ways of finding it out in the natural course of events. I daresay he knew when the deal was closed, and announced it accordingly.

That is an awfully innocent statement. Does the minister not know that the whole thing was done to have the effect that the provincial government of Nova Scotia had paved the way for this new industry?
The hon. gentleman says so, but certainly I do not know anything of the kind.
Why was it announced in that way?
Why was it announced in that way? I do not know.

Why was it not announced by the minister of munitions?

The War-Munitions and Supply

Our announcements come
through the publicity branch whenever we sign a contract, and I suppose this one went through in the usual way. I like to be accused of playing politics by hon. members who seem to think of nothing else; all I have heard from this section is, "Why don't you put something in the maritimes?" I have said repeatedly that I do not care where I put these things so long as I get the materials of war.

After discussing steel and ships and housing, I wonder whether we can come back to the matter of steel. I am not certain that I understood correctly the minister's statement with regard to whether or not there is a serious shortage of steel in Canada. I wish he would make himself a little clearer on that point. We do know that we have a steel priority in this country, and I assume that it is necessitated by shortage of steel. In that connection might I suggest something which will be of some little benefit to the western farmer. The suggestion comes to me that, on account of the present priority method of distributing steel, the men who run the small engineering shops experience tremendous difficulty in getting any. That has caused a serious situation for the farmers of western Canada during the time of harvest when they need repairs. I know for a fact that many have been held up in their operations because the local machine shop would not take care of their repairs, being unable to get a reasonable amount of steel, even though only a small bit was required, the shop being a small one. Of course, we in this corner realize that the farmer has been handicapped time and again, and it is another reason for dissatisfaction when he discovers that he cannot get repairs for machinery. It is a little late now to talk of that in connection with farming operations; nevertheless it seems to be true that the small shop is unable to get a reasonable amount of steel. Would the minister throw some further light on the priority arrangement in Canada with regard to steel?

This continent as well as every country at war is short of steel; in other words, we could use a good deal more than we can make. I believe we are getting along fairly well with our war programme notwithstanding that we are short on steel. If we had more forgings at the present time we would be making more guns, and if we had more plate we would get on faster with our shipbuilding programme.
