We are, however, bringing new capacity into production each month, which will tend to ease that situation, and as far as the war is concerned 
we have a reasonably balanced programme as between steel production and such imports of the finished product as we can count on from the United States. As far as non-war use is concerned, at present no steel is being allocated for such purposes. We have shut off a great number of types of manufacturing that depend upon steel, not because we wish to do so but because we cannot afford the steel. I daresay the farmer has been considerably inconvenienced on that account. We hope to be able by the spring to relieve the shortage in machine shops doing non-war work. At present we cannot do so because we are trying to allocate steel as carefully as we can in order to make it go as far as possible for essential war purposes in Canada.

I should hate to have the words of the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black) go unnoticed, and I wish particularly to meet two impressions which he left. The first is that we have no shipbuilding in Nova Scotia, that all that we have is a projected shipbuilding programme at Pictou. There is shipbuilding in Nova Scotia in mine sweepers, Fairmile vessels, scows, and the like, and they are building slips in different places on the shore for ship repairing. Repairs are going on in Halifax as well, and their yards are working to capacity. It is not fair for anyone to rise in his place in the house and leave the impression that Nova Scotia is forgotten altogether. I cannot let it go at that; I cannot allow the impression to remain that there is merely a projected programme at Pictou. There is considerable shipbuilding going on in my constituency, and at Weymouth, on the border of my constituency, we have one of the best Fairmile ship yards in Canada. At another place we have a number of mine sweepers and the like. Moreover, the hon. member made reference to political reactions that might arise and that were hoped for by the announcement of the projected plan of shipbuilding at Pictou. The only constituency in Nova Scotia that lost a Liberal to a Conservative was Pictou, so that it is plain to be seen, if one follows that suggestion to its logical conclusion, that any announcement that was made did not have the effect suggested. If anything, it worked the other way. The hon. member should be the last one to give the impression to the committee that in a particular declaration benefit was sought. As a matter of fact, the results went the other way.

I was referring to a principle in the announcement. I was referring to merchant steel shipbuilding.

The War-Munitions and Supply

The minister in his report
last Tuesday said, as reported at page 4082 of Hansard:
Capital assistance to industry for the extension of existing plants and for the construction of new plants, instalment of equipment, et cetera, aggregated a total of $550,000,000, partly for Canada, partly for the United Kingdom and partly for joint account.
Will the minister break down these figures and tell us when he can how much of that amount was for Canadian account, how much for United Kingdom account and how much for joint account? Will he also break down the figures so as to show how much was allotted to each province in Canada?
Mr. HOWE.:	Just before the last adjournment of parliament I gave a break-down with regard to Canadian, British and joint account. It runs pretty well in the same proportion. I will bring that up to date later on; I have not the figures before me. As regards a breakdown by provinces, that is a purely political question which we have refrained from answering, and I do not think I should care to compare expenditures province by province.

I understood the minister
to say that the government was financing some of these shipyards. Earlier in the year the policy announced by the minister was that all that financing was being left to private industry. Has the policy been changed? If so, about when was it changed, and how many shipyards are now being financed by the government?

There is no shipyard that is
really being financed by the government. That is rather a misstatement. In connection with the merchant shipbuilding programme, it was necessary to build a number of new berths. The general policy was to include the capital expenditure in the contract and to allow that to be written off for the first five boats with the understanding that when they were built the cost would be dropped accordingly. I think in one or two instances the capital sum was advanced to cover the improvement. In any event it was allowed to be written off over a certain amount of work, or advanced direct. I think that was done for practically every shop where an expansion of programme was involved. '

The same question comes up in connection with power. The minister, speaking to the Canadian Manufacturers' association on June 10 of this year, said:
We are accustomed to think of Canada as a country of large reserves of electric power. To-day every kilowatt that can be generated is being used.
14873-267i
He went on to explain the attempts being made to overcome the shortage. Is that still the position? Are we short of power right across Canada? If so, has consideration been given to the government financing the development of further power? Is that a government policy?

We have not financed any
power development in Canada since the beginning of the war.

Is the position that we have now reached the limit of our available power in Canada, that all power that has been developed is in use? If so, it would seem that some step should be taken to develop further power either by private industry or by the government, because the water and the power sites are there; it is simply a matter of harnessing the water.

Power is being developed
privately, and while every kilowatt available is being used, we are not exactly at the end of- our resources, because we can cut off peace-time use to some extent and convert it to war-time use. We are about on the borderline now. Of course this is the time of year when the domestic load is the heaviest. I think there will not need to be much diversion; there have been some instances in Ontario where peace-time loads have been cut off for certain parts of the day, but I do not think it will be serious this winter. A year from now it may be more serious. On the other hand, nearly a million horse power will come in between now and perhaps a year from now, which will relieve the situation.

For example, at the Bridge river site in British Columbia there is a partial development, but I think there is a potential of several hundred thousand horse power. Is there not some way by which the government could have that developed? Surely the power controller, or some department of government could have that done, or are we just to be bogged down waiting for private industry to move?

The government decided
early not to develop power. We had to decide what we would do and what we would not do. We decided we would not develop power, drill oil-wells-
Oil-wells are different; that is speculative; but the power site is there, it is only a matter of putting in the plant.

The owners of that site are
well able to develop it if they can sell the power.

The War-Munitions and Supply

I was pleased to hear that
there was so much shipbuilding going on in Nova Scotia. As I remember the last discussion, there was an appropriation of 150,000,000 for shipbuilding, and one per cent of that went to Nova Scotia. At that time we discussed the possibility of utilizing, I think, some twenty-five shipyards in Nova Scotia that were too small to handle the type of ships required. The minister stated that there was considerable activity in the building of lifeboats and small craft of that kind. To what extent are the shipyards in Nova Scotia being used for that purpose? As I go through the province I see very little shipbuilding activity.

I know that a large number of the ships are being built there; I would think every shipyard that wants a government contract and is able to do the work efficiently has all the work it can do. Of course there are yards that prefer to keep to the ordinary peace-time work rather than take war work. I cannot give the number of boats being built in Nova Scotia under the small-boat programme, but it is a large number; we have let contracts for some seven or eight hundred boats of that type to date.

Has consideration been given to taking the boats from Churchill? There are four that have been laid up there for the last three years, steel hull boats in good condition. Two of them at least could be used.

Consideration has been given to that. I know those boats very well. The tug at Churchill is of a type of which there is no particular shortage; it is not an oceangoing tug. As to the other equipment there, we have not been able to see value for taking it out of Churchill and having to take it back later when it will be required.
When will it be required there?
Dredging has to be done there from time to time, and we cannot operate a dipper dredge without a tug and three or four scows.

What progress has been made with regard to the "bits and pieces" programme? In western Canada, and particularly in Saskatchewan, there are many machine shops tolerably well equipped, many of them with machine tools and having a nucleus of anywhere from four to ten skilled employees, and particularly at this season of the year there is a dearth of employment for shops of that kind. These shops are anxious

to render service at this time. It is true they have been inspected from time to time, their tools listed, their equipment checked over, and their personnel passed upon. We who live in the west have regretfully come to the conclusion that the eastern industrialist who has a war order practises the British maxim, "What we have we hold," and is unwilling to pass out to other shops the right to manufacture component parts of the completed product. Could the minister indicate to the committee what organization has been set up for the "bits and pieces" programme and what hope our shops in western Canada may have of participating in the war programme in the months to come?

Our "bits and pieces" programme is well organized and is, I think, meeting the needs of industries of the kind to which my hon. friend refers. We have a district office in Winnipeg, and I think in Calgary, as well as in the eastern centres. Of course there are two sides to this question. I know the aeroplane plant at Fort William was carrying its "bits and pieces" as far west as Calgary in an endeavour to place contracts. My experience leads me to believe that the difficulty is more concerned with the little shop looking for work than with the larger plants trying to place work. One can hardly expect a large plant to distribute its work to every machine shop in the province; one might more reasonably expect the owner of the small machine shop to come to Winnipeg, discuss the matter and see what work is available. The "bits and pieces" programme is, however, succeeding as the small manufacturer becomes sufficiently interested to do what the large manufacturer has to do in obtaining an order, namely, come where the order is being placed and "sell" his capacity. I think we are educating the large manufacturer to break down his orders. There is a large contract just getting under way in Regina which I think can be very easily broken down into "bits and pieces"; but there again it will be necessary for the operator of the small machine shop to go to Regina and show what he can do, in order to obtain the work. I do not think anyone can sit back and expect the "bits and pieces" programme to bring him work.

Just what function is the office in Winnipeg supposed to perform? Does the contract holder or the manufacturer list with the Winnipeg office those component parts which he desires manufactured outside the plant? It is exceedingly difficult for the operator of a small machine plant, say at Wynyard, Saskatchewan, to know what component parts are required in connection with the production of an aeroplane, let us say.

The War-Munitions and Supply
What he desires is some central place where he can obtain that information and where the size of his shop, his equipment and his personnel can be listed.

That is exactly the purpose of the Winnipeg office, to obtain from the manufacturers the components they would like to place, and to obtain from the small machine shop the type of work it is capable of doing. I think that programme has been carried farther in Quebec than in any other province, because there seem to be more small machine shops in Quebec than in the other provinces; and through the "bits and pieces" programme I think we have pretty well filled the entire field there. A programme of education is being carried out on both sides, with the large manufacturer being educated to break down his production and sublet, while on the other hand the operator of the small machine shop is being educated to sort out what he is capable of doing and what he cannot handle.

What protection have the subcontractors with regard to receiving payment? I ask this question because a contract was let down on the lake shore in 1940; lumber contractors sold lumber to the man who had the contract, and they have not been paid as yet. What chance has a subcontractor of being paid? Does the government check on that?

As one who has had to do with government contracts over a great many years, I can say from experience that the government never pays a contractor in full as long as there is any claim or lien outstanding. If the suppliers of that contractor failed to notify the government that they had claims, I am afraid their recourse against the government is gone.

The government did hold back $7,000 on this contract, but I believe the contractor was paid $70,000 and he owed his subcontractors over $20,000. I believe one of those subcontractors has received about $1,200. Another lumber man is minus twelve or fifteen hundred dollars, and as far as I can see there is no chance of these men getting paid, because the contractor would be better off not to try to collect the $7,000 from the government.
How about the contractor who got the contract; is he bankrupt?

I
believe he is pretty close to it.

Unless a man protects his position on a government contract, I do not think he can be any better off in selling to a contractor who has a government contract than in selling to anyone else. The nature of contracting has not changed over the years, and ordinarily a person supplying a contractor must protect his position or he has no position.
My question has not yet been answered. I think the government should look after the subcontractors.
What relation is there between the government and a subcontractor?

The subcontractors believed this .man, having a government contract, would pay them; they thought he was honest and that the government would see that they got paid. In this instance they are holding the bag, while these other fellows are profiting by it.

Perhaps they had better see their lawyers, but certainly I can say that if the government is notified of a claim, sufficient money is always held back before final settlement, provided the claim can be shown to be proper.
The government has been notified about this.

speechtext: I think we have had a very exhaustive discussion concerning the Department of Munitions and Supply, and I wonder whether we could not proceed to the next department.

Before we do that, I should like some further assurance from the minister with respect to the breakdown of that expenditure of $550,000,000 to build plants, partly for Canadian and partly for United Kingdom account, requested by the hon. member for St. John-Albert. The information was promised 'by the minister, and I should like to know if we might have it before this part of the session ends. On February 25 the minister submitted an appendix to Hansard showing a total expenditure of $268,499,894. The expenditure under this heading has reached $550,000,000, and the information concerning it is of the greatest importance. I would support what was said by the hon. member for St. John-Albert in requesting that this information be placed on Hansard in the same form that was followed last February.

I will have that information prepared just as quickly as possible, and will try to get it on Hansard this session.

The War-Munitions and Supply

The minister will remember that last session we discussed the possibility of extending the air lines, both passenger and mail, to the city of Sydney, Nova Scotia. At that time the minister said there was a possibility that this service would be so extended by August of this year. Has any progress been made in that direction, or has the matter been forgotten?

No, it has not been forgotten; as a matter of fact, it is very close to coming into being. I think the difficulty was that we had so many urgent demands for the beam equipment that we intended to use there. We had to obtain emergency beam equipment in connection with the Newfoundland airports, and we are a little behind in that programme. I hope that by the new year we shall be flying planes to Sydney, but again that is subject to new calls for equipment. We are, however, doing our best.
Thank you. We are beginning to get linked up with Canada at last.

On November 4 the minister was discussing what he called the "bits and pieces" programme. He will recall that I asked a specific question, and I hope in the intervening six days he has had an opportunity to prepare a specific answer, or in any event to give the country a general statement as to the policy which his department intends to pursue in that regard. Only to-day an example of what I had in mind at that time came to my attention; I will recite the instance in order that the minister may give us any policy he may have with regard to the question I asked.
The question I asked on November 4, was: In respect of capital assistance is it the policy of the Department of Munitions and Supply to extend1 liquid capital or working capital to those industries which find themselves with a backlog of orders for ordinary business? If I may amplify my question, I would say that manufacturing institutions find very large priority orders coming in for munition manufacture, business which has to do with the Department of Munitions and Supply. Of course they must give first attention to those priorities, with the result that the normal shipments of commodities have to stand back until the priorities are filled. What is the position with regard to these small concerns about which the minister spoke on November 4, and concerning which I asked that simple and easily answered question?
They find, in connection with their capital structure that it is taking more money even in their normal business procedure to carry

their accounts receivable, to carry their inventory, to carry their raw materials, and to carry any stock they have ready for sale in the ordinary routine of business. The net result is that they are short of working capital. While they are in that position, a demand is being made on them to extend their plants, and they are anxious to answer those demands. Arrangements are made at present within the Department of Munitions and Supply to take care of that fixed assets cost, or capital assistance. But the policy as to what might be done with regard to working capital ought to be brought up to date by the minister, so that they would know what they are to do.
Many of these small industries have been established for two or three decades, and in taking on this war business, business which may be here to-day and gone to-morrow, they do not want to lose their old established lines. I have in mind an instance in Toronto which has to do with sandpaper. Sandpaper and buffing wheels are required for the polishing of rifle butts, et cetera. In this particular instance all other orders had to wait until that priority war older was turned out. In the meantime, furniture factories, and other plants throughout Canada which required sandpaper, could not be supplied. Some of the sandpaper may have been supplied for what might be described as semi-war work, but a good deal of it was for ordinary routine business. I use sandpaper only as an example. The people in question find themselves without the supply they require. Those who are charged with the responsibility of seeing to it that Canada has a sufficient supply of their commodity would be quite anxious to help out by building a temporary plant to take care of the condition which has developed.
I would ask the government to recite its general policy with regard to a problem of that kind, in respect of the capital structure of the extension which would have to be built. I would ask that in answering that question, particular attention be given to the write-off. In other words, if a building were of temporary construction to last for five years, would there be an increase in depreciation write-off on such building? I would not suggest that it need necessarily be 20 per cent, because there would, no doubt, be some reclamation. If an answer could be given, people who are having difficulties in that connection would have some peace of mind with regard to actual capital expenditure.
We may have to go a good deal further in extending working capital to take care of the three items I had in mind. My purpose in rising at this time is to ask the minister if he will answer the question I asked him in

The War-Munitions and Supply
good faith on November 4. I ask him to recite the policy so that those who are trying to do a job on behalf of Canada in respect of our "war effort will have some confidence that they may receive reasonable assistance from the government with regard to the war section of their business, and so that they may see to it that priorities are not dodged, and are given the right of way during the war.

The policy of the government in relation to capital assistance is that it extends capital assistance to its own contractors. That is, if a firm takes a large contract from the government, and requires building accommodation and/or machinery which it has not at present installed, under certain circumstances the government will provide the building and install the machinery, provided that the company will transfer the property on which the building stands, and the title of ownership, and the government will retain ownership of the building and the machinery. This type of assistance is extended only to prime contractors. I believe my hon. friend is referring to subcontractors, and to a case where a subcontractor is responsible to a main contractor.
I am referring more particularly to "bits and pieces."

"Bits and pieces" usually involve the breaking down of a main contract into subcontracts, which represent the "bits and pieces." Therefore there is no advance directly from the government to the "bits and pieces" man. We never advance money to a subcontractor, although sometimes we do advance money to a main contractor which will be spent with a subcontractor. That is an advance to the main contractor, because it must be his responsibility, which he passes on to the subcontractor. That is the policy with regard to capital expenditure.
In respect of our general policy, each case is examined to see whether an advance is justified, or whether it is a situation which a contractor should take care of by himself. Of course, if the contractor spends his own money, he has the privilege of appearing before the war contracts depreciation board, upon which occasion Mr. Justice McTague and his colleagues decide the post-war value of the improvements to be built. They determine the amount of the write-off and the period over which the write-off can be made.
In the matter of capital advances, it is against the policy of the department to make advances for working capital. Sometimes it has to be done. We may find that a firm taking a contract does not appear to have adequate working capital, or for one reason or another may find itself short of working capital. In that event it is always our practice to put a controller into the company to watch income and expenditures. Under such circumstances we do advance money. We have controllers in twelve or fifteen businesses in Canada to-day to watch working capital. But it is a difficult business to follow, and we avoid it as much as possible.

Will the minister bring up to date the statement given by his deputy before one of the committees which sat four or five months ago with respect to the amount of working capital advanced by his department?
I shall place that figure before the committee.

I have one further question, which is not entirely confined to the Department of Munitions and Supply. Due to the placing of ceiling prices on large numbers of commodities, a condition has arisen whereby raw materials for such commodities still being exported to the United States are finding a market in the United States ranging anywhere from 10 to 50 per cent higher than the market which prevails at the ceiling rate in Canada. For example, manufacturers for years have tried to make their contracts for one year, but latterly it has been for six or three months. The raw material for the commodity they manufacture is under contract to December 31, 1941; the producer of the primary product now finds himself under the September 15 ceiling, and the man who buys from him is unable to increase his price to meet the competition which comes from the United States. The goods are exportable to the United States. The net result of it all is that before 1942 is over, there is going to be a large shortage of raw material. Certainly it is going to be very difficult to contract for raw material for the year 1942. Those supplying raw material who have in days gone by intermittently exported their commodity to the United States have latterly, due to business being considerably improved in the last year, found their market in Canada during the year 1941. Naturally they will want to revert to the high United States market again. General market conditions in the United States, as the minister well knows, are anywhere from 10 to 50 per cent higher than in Canada, and in the instance I mentioned, the market is from 90 to 100 per cent higher. The quantities I am thinking of run into millions of pounds.
*4240

The War-Munitions and Supply
Contract time is fast approaching, December being the month when contracts for the year 1942 are made. There has been no announcement of policy as to how the government proposes to hold and maintain this ceiling. Priorities on supplies for war contracts must be taken care of. Certain industries will find themselves denuded of their supplies of raw material. The problem is approaching dimensions which may give our government some concern.
One way out, of course, would be to lift the ceiling on the finished product. But we do not want to do that. There will probably be no ceiling for that portion of material which goes into war products, but one cannot reasonably sell a product at one price to a customer who has been on your books for twenty or thirty years and is operating a necessary industry, and sell the same product to some other industry which is engaged on "bits and pieces" or any sort of munitions work and expect that one will have anything but chaos in that particular industry. I admit that the problem is a difficult one, but I think the Department of Munitions and Supply should be apprised of what they are going to be faced with during the year 1942, and I would appreciate it if the Minister of Munitions and Supply or some other minister would make a statement on the matter before the house adjourns until January, so that the year 1942 will not find the entire situation upset.
To follow it along a little further, what actually happens to-day is this. Many large United States industries have branch plants in Canada, and these branch plants interchange raw material between the branch plants and the main plant in the United States. The branch plants try to concentrate on one line of manufacture, and they may gather up in Canada the raw material for half a dozen lines of manufacture of similar commodities. There may be as many as twenty factories between Canada and the United States using probably twenty different kinds of raw material. In one city they would concentrate on the manufacture of one grade of raw material, another in Buffalo, another in Chicago, and so forth, and concentrate on another manufacture in Montreal, another in Brantford, and another in Toronto. Thus the raw material is flowing back and forth all the time. My question is, where is it going to flow to? If the prevailing market in the United States has no ceiling on it,, which is the condition that obtains to-day, it offers a much better market, and are we going to be handicapped and embarrassed to a degree by

the manufacture of munitions and the hundreds and thousands of supplies of all sorts which come under the purview of the minister?

The problem put forward by my hon. friend the member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) is not a new one. Exports are controlled by export licences in lines where there is a threatened shortage for Canadian purposes. At the present time licences are required for the export of any steel product, and licences have been required for a good while for the export of certain chemicals. It is the practice of our department, whenever a material gets in short supply, to place that material under the necessity of export licence.
In the matter of lumber we have a situation where we have no export licences because it has not been thought necessary. About fifty per cent of our lumber is consumed in Canada, I suppose, and about fifty per cent is exported. What is exported brings prices anyvrhere from twenty to forty per cent higher than can be obtained by sale in Canada. One might say that that is a case where we must exercise export control, but as a matter of fact the industry is regulated by a controller, and the controller, by agreement with the industry, has provided that as long as the industry will supply to Canada at pegged prices the lumber required in Canada, it is quite welcome to export the remainder. The trade have played the game; there has been no shortage of timber in Canada, and the industry has been able to market about fifty per cent of its product in the United States.
The steel situation requires control. If a dealer in Canada could buy a keg of nails and get an export permit,, he could sell it to any south American country for twice what he paid for it and never see the keg of nails. There, of course, is a situation which requires control, and we have control of the steel industry. Unless it can be shown that a manufacturer of steel products is supplying an old customer in a market that has always been his, he is not likely to get a permit for the export of steel from Canada to-day. That will be extended perhaps to all products in Canada as the pegged price in Canada tends to spread from the prices abroad.

Perhaps I should take the time of the committee to put on the record this letter which came to my attention only this morning. I have not been given permission to use the name of the writer, and therefore I shall omit that. The letter

The War-Munitions and Supply
is dated November 5, 1941. I asked my question on November 4, the day preceding. The letter reads as follows:
We have been offered extremely good prices for shipment of ... to the United States.
We realize and appreciate the fact that we have been shipping to you for some time at prices that were established in January, 1941, but in view of the present price ceiling we are unable to ask you to quote prices that would compete with our American buyer.
We would ask you, however, if you are willing to allow us to ship certain quantities of this raw material to the above-mentioned buyer in the United States. . . .
I am not going to mention the name.
. . . and if you would consider this would you kindly advise what proportion you would consider releasing for the American market?
Unfortunately we did not review our prices earlier and hence we are saddled with fixed prices which we do not believe are in line with what was readily obtainable in the basic period, September 15 to October 11.
We know that a number of people are in the same boat and of course it will take some time before adjustments are made to take care of this ceiling price.
We hope you will consider what we have requested and trust that you can give us an early reply.
That particular contract represents fifty-two carloads of material, and that is only a portion of a total of 19,000 tons. This firm which is in the same boat happens to be connected directly with the sandpaper industry. All I ask is that some recital of policy be given, so that the relationships between contractors, manufacturers and their sources of supply will not be disrupted too much.

I think I can say with confidence that if my hon. friend will notify the proper controller, either in the Department of Munitions and Supply or in the war-time prices and trade board, of his request, an export licence will be required for that material. The government will require to be convinced that there is sufficient for Canadian needs at the pegged price before any export whatever is permitted.

If I may return to the question of gas, which seems an appropriate subject here, I wonder whether the minister could tell us what has become of the Pogue carburettor- whether it is in the process of being put on the market?

I shared my hon. friend's interest in the Pogue carburettor at the time it was a subject of interest, and I know of the so-called experiments carried out with it in the west. The inventor of the carburettor finally found a wealthy sponsor in the person of Mr. J. E. Hammell, one of Canada's great
mining men. Mr. Hammell moved Mr. Pogue and the carburettor into his own estate near Toronto, fitted up a workshop for him, and took pains to see that the development was carried out by proper experts. Mr. Hammell has never been willing to quite say what happened to the Pogue carburettor, but he did say that he spent about $40,000 or $50,000 and decided that it could not be made a financial success. I can assure hon. members that there was no sinister influence from either the big oil companies or the automobile companies; they had nothing to do with it. Mr. Hammell took the thing in charge because those accusations were made and he wanted to have an independent inquiry and see what could be developed from it.

I rise at this hour of the evening, a quarter past ten, because at the present time there is a black-out in several cities of the province of Quebec, which are protected by adding darkness to darkness, by making the night blacker. The modern Joshuas do not stop the sun, as happened in the olden time, but they prevent the moon from shining-and it means that this country is well-protected!
What is the purpose of this black-out? It is to prevent the enemy from seeing military secrets which do not exist. If you remember, Mr. Chairman, last year, when I asked what kind of protection was accorded to the county of Temiscouata against any attack by land or sea or air, I had from the Minister of National Defence this insolent reply, "It is a military secret"-when there was no defence at all.
I find that this black-out business is a sinister joke on the Canadian people. What, sir, a black-out! And all that light shining on the St. Lawrence river? A black-out from here, a black-out from there, a little space of darkness on the lights of my province or on the lights of any province in Canada!
The Minister of Munitions and Supply gave us figures about the production of armaments in this country. I do not believe what he says; I believe what I see, and I see nothing. Let us go up the tower of this building and look round the roof of this building, or the roof of the east block, the west block, the confederation building, the justice building, or any other of hundreds of buildings round here; how many anti-aircraft guns are there? None. They are well hidden; it is a military secret; there are none. Where is the member of parliament who has seen one anti-aircraft gun in Ottawa or in any other city of this dominion? There are none. Yet we hear of millions, hundreds of millions of dollars being spent for munitions and supplies; we hear of

The War-Munitions and Supply
this from the mouth of the minister, and on paper, and in the stupid propaganda of the bureau of information. As a Canadian I am fed-up with that. "Black-out" means protection against the enemy who is coming to invade this country, and what protection have we in Canada? None. All our munitions are going abroad-meaning that Canada does not need to be defended, that eastern Canada where I live and where many people live, does not need to be protected. I submit it is an absurdity.
What about these corporations a VitaUenne and these commissars a la russe that infest the Departments of Munitions and Supply? During the last war, when Sir Robert Borden was in power, at the time of the union government, there was only one man handling all the business in which there is now such a mix-up. That man has been honoured by the king; he is a former colleague and a very dear friend of mine; he is the lieutenant-governor of the province of Quebec, Major-General Sir Eugene Fiset, formerly deputy minister of national defence, at a time when there was no such mess as the Department of Munitions and Supply, against which I protested at the start. He alone handled all the business. How is it that at that time one man from Quebec, Major-General Sir Eugene Fiset, whom we all respect, could do the work of all those nonentities who are now in the Department of Munitions and Supply, and who never cease to pass regulations which swear at each other all the time? The minister cannot say anything against General Fiset because he saved his skin in the committee of railways, canals and telegraph lines when he replaced the deputy speaker, the chairman of the committee of the whole. Sir Eugene Fiset was a good man; he is still a good man; he is lieutenant-governor of Quebec. It took hundreds or thousands of people to replace that man. During the time of the Borden government and the union government, Sir Robert Borden was strong enough to put Sam Hughes out and to replace him with General Mewburn, which showed his strength, his determination and his firm will to have an able man at the head of the department.
I am a Liberal; I have never been a Tory and I never will be, although I have many friends on the Conservative side. But in time of war there should be freedom of speech and one should never be afraid to tell the truth. As a Canadian, I should be ashamed of myself if I took for granted all that is said by the minister. My eyes cannot deceive me. Where is the member of parliament who has seen aircraft here in action over parliament hill? There was a display of [Mr. Pouliot.l
floodlights some time ago, but none of those who were operating those lights could find the aeroplanes that were in the sky, and an aeroplane had to come into the middle of the beam of light, it had to expose itself, in order to be seen.
The law of the land is the mobilization act, which provides for the defence of Canada. We should be defended, but we are not now. All sentimentality should cease. I have had enough of bed-time stories. I want to see some of these guns, some of that ammunition that we hear so much about and never see. I want to see every part of the country well defended; I want to see the Department of Munitions and Supply serving some purpose. I do not want it only to give an opportunity to some capitalists to receive subsidies that are so high, higher even than the amount issued to the public for the building of a dry dock or anything of that sort.
I will not "dot the i's" to-night. It will be enough to mention some schemes floated along at the expense of the public for the building of a dry dock, a ship, or plants adjacent thereto. The issue was so much and they received from the Department of Munitions and Supply a subsidy so high that not only did it cover the issue but there was a surplus; and those who received such subsidies were embarrassed. They did not know whether they were to distribute the surplus as dividends to shareholders of the company, or remit it to the public treasury. Moreover, there was a depreciation of fifty per cent per annum which was supplied to that company. It is not surprising that we have a lot of expenditures now. What amount is spent for England; what amount is spent for Canada; what is protected by the black-out? We have a right to know, and if the minister cannot answer in public but repeats again the eternal story that it is a military secret, then let us sit in camera. Let us clear the galleries and let us get true information.
Members of parliament should be relied upon as much as any business man who comes here to make money in the Department of Munitions and Supply and to organize trusts. I said-and it was not denied either by the Minister of National Defence or by the Minister of Munitions and Supply before the last adjournment-that on the treasury benches there were men who wanted to organize Italian corporatism, Italian fascism in Canada. I am for democracy, and I regret that my hon. friend from Parkdale is not in his seat. But members must recollect that when it was desired to have the hon. gentleman who was in the chair-he was not you, sir-prevent the hon. member for Parkdale

The War-Munitions and Supply
from speaking, I said: "Let him speak; I will answer him afterwards; but both of us must be given freedom." That is what I understand by Liberalism, and my freedom of speech shall not be curtailed by anyone in this house. I was here a long time before the pontiffs of materialism who are now handling the business of this country in certain departments, and what I think is that the human lives of my constituents and the lives of other citizens in Canada are worth more than any pile of money, worth more than any of those earthly treasures that some people seem to appreciate so much. If the people of Canada are ready to make the supreme sacrifice in the defence of this land, there should be a general clean-up in the Augean stables of the Department of Munitions and Supply.

I do not quite agree with the Minister of Pensions and National Health when he says that we have exhausted this department. I do not think that we can exhaust that department or exhaust the minister even though some of us would like to exhaust the whole government. I wonder whether the Minister of Munitions and Supply would give the committee the procedure that is followed when the government buys land on which to establish an air training school. Mv understanding is that the government have their agents out looking for desired sites. The agent will go to the owner of the land, who may be a farmer. I suppose most of the land is owned by fawners, and the agent will dicker with the farmer. He will tell the farmer that the government is going to establish an air training school here, that this particular property has been chosen for the school and that the government must have it. Perhaps he asks the farmer how much he wants for his land. The tendency may be for an individual to say then, "Well, now, here is a chance to make a little money." I suppose that is sometimes done. Anyway, the farmer will quote his price; the agent will say, "Oh, that is much too much," and the agent then will suggest how much the land is worth, which perhaps is about half what the farmer asks for. Then there will come bargaining one with the other. I am told that these agents will say to the farmers, "Well, now, there is no use in your bucking the government; the government is going to take the land anyway. Of course, if you want to go to court about it, that is your own business." But no farmer wants to go to court against the government; he thinks he will not win the ease anyhow, so eventually he is brought to a place where he will accept what is offered. The agent reports to his superiors and the deal is closed. Would the
minister tell us just what happens when an agent reports to his superiors what the land has been offered for? If there is a board of arbitration has the minister any record of the board raising the ante on the farmer and giving more than he asked? Perhaps it would be in order on some occasion to ask for a return of the amounts paid for these parcels of land; however, I am not interested in that for the moment. Would the minister tell us exactly what the procedure is? I have in mind the case of a man who claims to have been paid half what his property was really worth.

The Department of Munitions and Supply arranged with the Canadian National Railways that the experienced land department of that railway would acquire the lands needed by the department, and that practice 'has been followed in all our land purchases. Mr. Clark, the head of the land department of the national railway, with his staff, has made all the arrangements. My hon. friend gave the procedure. Of course, before any land is purchased, the government is free to act, and the usual practice is, I think, to test out the value of land in that area by endeavouring to make actual purchases. If that is done and it is not possible to complete the purchase by offer and acceptance, then expropriation is proceeded with, and the reluctant seller has the choice of going before the exchequer court and taking the value placed by the court or settling with the government. Sometimes one course is followed, sometimes another. I have heard many criticisms of prices paid for land, but as far as western Canada is concerned the criticism has seldom been that the price was too low. I think my hon. friend will find that usually it is well above the normal price in the area.
Is it necessary that plans be signed by the Minister of National Defence for Air and the commandant in that area before an airport is constructed?
Oh, yes.
Is it never done otherwise?
No.

Have any steps been taken to set up a steel rolling mill in British Columbia? As I understand, there is no way of disposing of scrap iron there unless it is sent to the United States; yet many cargo vessels are being built for which steel has to be imported, and steel will be needed there for a long time. Would it not be worth while for the government to put in a rolling mill or whatever plant is necessary to make use of that local supply?

The War-Munitions and Supply

The government never builds mills of that kind itself. It will assist in the financing of a mill, and I have offered to do that on one or two occasions with those who take an interest in the situation at Vancouver, but the matter has never been followed up. There are difficulties; Vancouver is ordinarily a sort of dumping ground for the eastern mills. Ordinarily the price of steel products in Vancouver is lower than in Sydney or in Hamilton where the steel is made, and all the companies seem to compete in that area. It is very doubtful whether an industry put there at this time could succeed in peace time.
As far as building steel ships goes, the contribution of an electric furnace would be of very little use, only to make castings suitable for bolts and nuts and foundry work of that kind. It could not make ship plates or ship shapes or any of the highly finished products. The small capacity furnace that would be warranted by the amount of scrap available in British Columbia would be neither here nor there. We would like a small supply of that type of steel on the west coast, and my offer is still open if we can find anyone willing to risk their own money in the venture and supply the management.

In connection with land purchases, is the actual contract negotiated with the assistance of officers of the crown, or has the department lawyers in the employ of the government in the various provinces?

The actual negotiations are
carried out by the land department of the railway. In acquiring the title we apply to the Department of Justice for legal assistance, and if they have an officer in the area they usually refer it to that officer; if not, they choose a solicitor, usually convenient to the area, who conducts the search and certifies the title.

Is there a board of
arbitration at all?
No.

The other day when the Minister of National Defence for Air was speaking he described the repair and overhaul of aeroplanes as a troublesome problem. What facilities are available in western Canada for the repair and overhaul of aeroplanes? What policy is pursued? If it is done in large centres or central plants, where are those plants located and what capital assistance has been given towards their construction and equipment?
There are a number of aerodromes in western Canada, a number of schools being operated, and I understand there is a staff

in each of those aerodromes, varying from twenty to perhaps seventy mechanics, more or less proficient, who make minor repairs and who in course of time become so skilled in these repairs that they tell me they could take care of anything except the repair of a crashed plane. Does that come under the Department of Munitions and Supply, and would the department consider the extension of the plan, supplying each aerodrome with some additional equipment so that even more extensive repairs could be undertaken?
The other day the minister stated that the shortage of parts was a serious problem. What provision has the department made with regard to furnishing parts, and to what extent could the smaller machine shops throughout western Canada be used in the making of these repair parts? We have, as I said before, a large number of skilled mechanics in the west, I should have said still in the west. From week to week these men are being drained into industry in eastern Canada. Only some three weeks ago an advertisement appeared in all the western papers asking lathe men, grinders, borers and other skilled operators to apply to the employment agency, stating that their expenses would be paid to points in eastern Canada. I realize that the Minister of Munitions and Supply is most anxious to obtain a completed product, but we who live in the west dislike this continued migration of our skilled workers to other parts of Canada. Therefore I would once more urgently call to his attention the desirability of bringing industry, and a greater part of Canada's war effort, to the point where the labour can be found.

As far as the overhaul of planes is concerned, the Royal Canadian Air Force maintains an overhaul staff at each airport. A plane, of course, is overhauled almost every time it lands. It is checked out each morning after an inspection, and any minor repairs are made by the staff. The air force can expand these staffs as much as it wishes, but I think it has been found economical to have them do only the minor repairs. Any major overhaul, such as the tearing down of an engine, the repairing of a wing, or anything of that sort, is sent to one of the overhaul centres which are operated by the Department of Munitions and Supply. Each type of engine has its own overhaul plant, one in western Canada and one in eastern Canada. The engine would be sent to that plant, which has facilities for tearing it down, replacing any defective parts, rebuilding it and testing it for use. Similarly the planes are sent to certain major overhaul

The War-Munitions and Supply
depots where they are stripped down and where defective parts are replaced. There are a number of these depots in western Canada; two at Vancouver, one at Edmonton, one at Prince Albert, one at Moose Jaw and one at either Medicine Hat or Lethbridge. There is a very large one at Winnipeg.
Certainly the intention has been to repair in western Canada the planes used in western Canada. The plan we have followed in locating the major overhaul bases has been to expand existing industries. In Vancouver we had two pre-war repair industries; these have been expanded. We had an overhaul plant at Edmonton, which had been in existence for a good many years; that was expanded, and the same thing was done at Prince Albert and Moose Jaw. In Winnipeg we had MacDonald Brothers, which plant now has been expanded into a very large overhaul project. As my hon. friend has said, the repair of aeroplanes, both major and minor, is a very large and growing problem. I think I said in my statement that the major overhaul plants would handle about five thousand planes this year. Of course some planes would be handled two or three times, but nevertheless the number of planes requiring overhaul this year will be about five thousand. We estimate that next year the number of planes requiring overhaul in all Canada will be ten thousand, so this in itself has become a major industry.

There was a return brought down to-day showing the exports of steel scrap from British Columbia. Does the minister think it is good business on our part to allow steel scrap to be exported from British Columbia when it is so greatly required for the manufacture of steel in Canada? In answering that question, could the minister tell us what has become of the shipload of steel scrap that was on the ss. Boris, tied up at the Vancouver dock? My view is that no steel scrap should be exported from Canada, because every pound of it will be and is required for the manufacture of our steel.

It is all very well to say that not a pound of steel scrap should be exported from Canada, but we must remember that on balance we are importers of steel scrap to the extent of about five hundred thousand tons a year. There is no steel industry in Vancouver at the present time; in fact, to my knowledge there never has been a steel industry there. We have scrap in British Columbia, which is not an economical area for any steel consuming furnace. When we are asking the United States to give us scrap in the eastern area to the extent of about five hundred thousand tons a year-and I may
add that without this scrap we would not be able to conduct our steel operations at Sydney, Hamilton or Sault Ste. Marie at the present rate of production-it is very difficult for us to refuse to export to the United States scrap which is needed there and which is in an uneconomical area in Canada. You may say provincial politics will prevent it, if you like; nevertheless this is a national problem of great importance, and we are meeting it as we should meet national problems. In other words, we are allowing the scrap to move out of an uneconomical area for the sake of getting a very much larger tonnage of scrap in an economical area, where the scrap can be used for war purposes.
Has the minister any information regarding the 7,500 tons of steel scrap tied up in the Greek ship ss. Borist

Yes, I think the ship and its cargo of scrap are still at the dock. Our department is very much interested in both the ship and its cargo, but so far no means has been found of acquiring ownership. Greece, of course, is not an enemy of Canada; it is an ally, and as yet we have not been able to find a Greek government which can release the ship to Canada. We are hardly justified in seizing it from a friend, and we cannot buy it.

I should like to put on record an observation with regard to the matter discussed a moment ago by the hon. member for Regina. Perhaps the minister will be able to give some thought to it, or possibly he may be able to reply. In my opinion one branch of the Department of Munitions and Supply has not been given sufficient consideration; that is the branch having to do with the salvage, for example, from the five thousand planes the minister mentioned a moment or two ago. Quite a number of planes are not overhauled. As the minister knows, badly crashed planes are thrown into the corner until after the inquest and whatnot. They remain there for a considerable length of time and eventually find their way into ordinary scrap, aluminum, steel, or whatever it may be. I would not suggest for a moment that some branch of the air force, taking its advice from the Department of Munitions and Supply, should try to reclaim those parts to put in other planes, but I do believe that a very large quantity of parts of considerable value might find their way into the ordinary plant repairs and maintenance requirements of industry. They would be worth a good deal of money, much more than would be their value for salvage. On account of freight rates it is

The War-Munitions and Supply
difficult to move large quantities of salvage to points of consumption, but a large number of parts used in industry-because, after all, they are standard goods-could be put to useful purposes, and add to the general economy of Canada.
I believe, if the minister would have an investigation made at Uplands, he would find motors which may have been in crashes, and other parts of planes, left out so that they are rusting and spoiling. I would ask the minister to answer this portion of my question:	Is
there any branch in his department giving attention to the matter of salvage? Do not let there be any misunderstanding, I would not for one moment ask that the spare parts be put back into aeroplanes which are carrying people 10,000 feet up in the air. I would not ask that such a chance be taken. At the same time there is a market for those parts, and it seems to me that with the elaborate inspection system in the Department of Munitions and Supply they could be reclaimed and put back into service in industry, if not within the Department of Munitions and Supply itself.

The Department of Munitions and Supply has a scrap disposal division, but it deals more particularly with scrap from our own industry, such as turnings from shell castings and gun forgings. Crashed aeroplanes, however, are the property of the Royal Canadian Air Force. My hon. friend may know of instances where engines have been left out in the open. I would not question his knowledge, but I would assume that parts of engines are so badly needed as spare parts for the Royal Canadian Air Force that an engine would be reclaimed very quickly and stripped.
It is not being done to the extent it should be.

I shall be glad to take the matter up with our own aircraft department, and with my colleague the Minister of National Defence for Air, and we will see that it is done. I fully agree that it should be done. Of course, no property of the government can be sold, except through the salvage officer in the Department of Finance. That office is functioning. Any reclamation or sale of government property is carried on through it.

I should like to direct the attention of the minister to the matter of real estate, and I do so because I would expect him to be in ignorance of the case I shall place before him. After, however, I relate the circumstances, he may wish to have a chat with someone in his department

entrusted with the erection of buildings. In the Slocan valley at a point called Crestover there is a beam station. Two residences were constructed for those looking after the station. Each of those residences cost $9,000, and the director of housing in Ottawa told me that the average price for a six-roomed residence under the government plan is about $4,500.
The blue-prints and specifications in this instance constitute a huge volume more than an inch in thickness. Who the architect was, I do not know, but I would ask hon. members to follow the plans. Downstairs there are two bedrooms, a bathroom and a kitchen. There is also a combination livingroom and diningroom. Upstairs there are three bedrooms, but no bathroom. The joke is that the specifications call for a waterproof concrete foundation. The fact is, however, that two or three wells have been drilled to a depth of over 400 feet, and water has not been found.
I know the minister resents any suggestion of politics, but I must point out that within thirty miles of these buildings there resides a Montreal architect who moved to Kootenay West for the purpose of supervising and planning the construction of a $100,000 residence. His further capabilities were indicated by the fact that he was awarded a prize for the construction of the Canadian building at the world's fair. Nobody in the interior was given an opportunity either to review or to tender on the buildings. But the one who did get the contract was a man who had done most of the Liberal contracting in Kootenay West for the last twenty years, and he resides in Vancouver, 500 miles away.
This means that $9,000 was thrown away on those buildings. The two buildings could have been constructed for $9,000, instead of only one of them. The people resent this, when they stop to think that they are striving to meet the government's appeal for the purchase of war savings certificates and victory bonds. Surely the minister would admit that any repetition of such reckless and useless expenditure should not occur.
Houses of that type are built by the Department of Transport. They build a great many of them. I recognize the layout of the house described by the hon. member, because I have been in many of them.
The man upstairs could not take a bath, I suppose.

There is a full basement in those houses. They contain first-class heating plants, because they are usually built in remote areas. Of course they have complete plumbing. Because they are built in remote

Labour Conditions
areas they are of fireproof construction. I believe my hon. friend will agree that they are of either concrete or brick construction.
Mr. E8LING: No; they are frame.

I would be surprised to find that. The ones I have seen are of fireproof construction. I shall, however, look into the matter. May I point out that tenders are usually let. The plans are advertised in local papers. That is the procedure which has been followed by the Department of Public Works for many years, and I cannot imagine that the contractor would obtain very much more than the fair cost of the building. The plans may be extravagant, but, as I say, they are plans which have been adopted as being suitable for similar buildings in other parts of Canada. My hon. friend has, however, pointed out that this is a frame building, and for that reason I would be pleased to look into it, and perhaps give him some information with respect to it later.
I would ask for a reply to-morrow to the question I asked on November 4.

I will give it.
